Exchange becomes reasonable when compressions can continue during the attempt, or after ROSC, and only if there is a clear benefit (leak at higher pressures, need for protection, long transport).

In critically ill adults, cardiac arrest occurs in a few percent of emergency intubations, far more often than in the operating room. Severe hypoxaemia and cardiovascular collapse (a systolic pressure below about 65 mmHg or a new vasopressor requirement) are each common. Most arrests happen within minutes of induction and many are pulseless electrical activity or bradycardia.

Four mechanisms combine. Hypoxaemia from apnoea in a patient with poor reserve. Hypotension from loss of sympathetic tone with induction and reduced venous return from positive pressure. Worsening acidosis when a compensating patient becomes apnoeic and is then under-ventilated. And right-ventricular failure when hypoxia, hypercapnia and positive pressure raise pulmonary vascular resistance in a ventricle already at its limit.
Hypoxaemia: optimise pre-oxygenation with NIV or a PEEP valve, use apnoeic oxygenation, ventilate gently during apnoea if needed, and aim for first-pass success.

Hypotension: treat volume depletion with fluid or blood, start or increase a vasopressor infusion before induction (many teams target a systolic pressure above about 90–100 or MAP above 65 before proceeding), have push-dose vasopressors ready, and reduce the induction dose. Avoid propofol in shock.

Acidosis: minimise apnoea time; immediately after intubation set a minute ventilation matching the pre-intubation effort. Some clinicians consider bicarbonate in extreme acidaemia as a bridge, though evidence is limited.

RV failure: avoid hypotension and hypoxia; consider an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator if available; use modest PEEP and tidal volumes; consider awake or delayed approaches and the smallest possible induction dose.

Check pressure every one to three minutes after induction. If it falls: give a push-dose vasopressor, increase the infusion, reduce PEEP and tidal volume temporarily if positive pressure is limiting venous return, rule out tension pneumothorax and auto-PEEP by disconnecting briefly, and treat bleeding.

If the patient arrests, start high-quality CPR and follow ACLS, and look for reversible causes particular to this setting: hypoxia (tube position, DOPE), hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, acidosis, hyperkalaemia (succinylcholine in a susceptible patient), and auto-PEEP. Disconnecting the ventilator for 30–60 seconds treats breath stacking.

A 55-year-old after hip surgery with sudden dyspnoea: SpO₂ 84 % on a non-rebreather, BP 86/52, HR 128, distended neck veins, RV dilation on bedside ultrasound. He is tiring and the team considers intubation before transfer to a centre for catheter-directed therapy.

This patient is at extreme risk of arrest at induction: a failing, pressure-loaded right ventricle that depends on sympathetic tone and preload, combined with hypoxaemia. Positive pressure raises RV afterload and reduces venous return.

A tracheostomy is an opening into the trachea; the upper airway is still connected to the lungs. These patients can, in principle, be oxygenated from the mouth and nose, or intubated orally, once the stoma is covered.

A laryngectomy removes the larynx and brings the trachea out as an end stoma; there is no connection between the mouth and the lungs. Oxygen must go to the stoma. Oral intubation is impossible. Bedside signs, wristbands and the patient's own information should make clear which type you are dealing with.

Call for help, apply oxygen to both the face and the stoma, and assess patency. Remove any speaking valve or cap, remove the inner cannula if present (many blockages are in the inner tube), and pass a suction catheter. If the catheter passes easily, the tube is likely patent: continue assessment and ventilate.

If the catheter will not pass, deflate the cuff and reassess. If the patient is still not breathing adequately, remove the tracheostomy tube. Then oxygenate: for a tracheostomy, by standard upper-airway methods with the stoma covered, or via the stoma with a paediatric face mask or a laryngeal mask applied to the stoma; for a laryngectomy, via the stoma only.

Secondary steps: oral intubation (tracheostomy patients only) or intubation of the stoma with a smaller tracheostomy or endotracheal tube, ideally over a bougie or with a fibreoptic scope. A new or fresh tracheostomy (less than about 7 days) has an immature tract that may close or allow a false passage, so recannulation is riskier.

Angioedema: from ACE inhibitors (bradykinin-mediated, does not respond reliably to adrenaline or antihistamines), hereditary angioedema, or anaphylaxis (histamine-mediated, responds to IM adrenaline). Look for voice change, stridor, drooling and tongue or floor-of-mouth swelling. An awake fibreoptic nasal approach by an expert, with a surgical airway prepared, is often preferred when swelling is progressing.

Inhalation injury: soot in the airway, facial burns, singed nasal hair, hoarseness or stridor after fire in an enclosed space. Swelling progresses over hours, worsened by resuscitation fluids. Early intubation with a large tube (7.5–8.0 or more for bronchoscopy) before transport is often indicated when signs of airway involvement exist.

Penetrating neck trauma: an expanding haematoma can distort and compress the airway. Avoid blind techniques that may enter a false passage; consider an awake approach or early surgical airway with a surgeon present. Airway injury with air bubbling from the wound may be intubated directly through the wound in extremis.

Obesity: rapid desaturation, difficult mask ventilation and difficult surgical airway. Ramp, head up, pre-oxygenate with PEEP, use apnoeic oxygenation and video laryngoscopy, and mark the membrane by ultrasound if possible.

A 6-year-old with a tracheostomy on home ventilation becomes acutely distressed during transfer: SpO₂ 82 %, no chest rise with the ventilator, high-pressure alarms. Parents say the tube was changed yesterday and the stoma is mature.
The airway is probably blocked or displaced. Parents are a resource — they often know the tube size, how to change it, and the child's baseline.

A sustained, rectangular capnography waveform over several breaths confirms that the tube delivers gas to and from perfused lungs. Professional guidelines treat continuous waveform capnography as mandatory for confirmation and monitoring of every intubated patient, including during transport. "No trace = wrong place" until proven otherwise.

An oesophageal tube may briefly show CO₂ if the stomach contains exhaled gas from mask ventilation or carbonated drinks, but the trace decays to zero within a few breaths. A tube above the cords can show a trace but will leak and dislodge.

In cardiac arrest, CO₂ delivery to the lungs falls with low flow, but high-quality CPR usually produces a measurable, if low, waveform. A flat trace during CPR should prompt reassessment of tube position (visualise with the laryngoscope) rather than acceptance.

Visualising the tube pass through the cords is strong evidence at the time but does not protect against later displacement. Breath sounds are unreliable in noisy aircraft and may be transmitted from the stomach. Chest rise, misting of the tube and colorimetric CO₂ detectors support placement but are less reliable than waveforms. Ultrasound can show tracheal versus oesophageal placement and bilateral lung sliding. A chest X-ray shows depth, not tracheal versus oesophageal placement.

Oesophageal detector devices (bulb or syringe) are unreliable in obesity, pregnancy and with copious secretions. Pulse oximetry falls late after oesophageal intubation, particularly after good pre-oxygenation — saturation can remain high for minutes with the tube in the oesophagus.

In adults, a depth of about 21 cm at the incisors in women and 23 cm in men is typical; in children over about two years, three times the tube size or (age ÷ 2) + 12 cm at the lips. Confirm bilateral air entry and, when available, imaging or ultrasound. Document the depth and recheck it after every move.
Neck flexion moves the tube tip toward the carina; extension moves it toward the cords. In small children a few centimetres of movement can extubate or cause mainstem intubation.

Cuff pressure should be about 20–30 cmH₂O, measured with a manometer. Over-inflation causes tracheal mucosal ischaemia; under-inflation allows aspiration and leak. At altitude in unpressurised cabins, air in the cuff expands; check and adjust.

Keep capnography connected from intubation to handover. A sudden loss of the waveform means displacement, disconnection or obstruction until proven otherwise; a sudden fall to a low value suggests cardiac arrest or massive embolism; a gradual rise suggests hypoventilation or rising metabolism; a "shark-fin" upstroke suggests bronchospasm or obstruction.
Before every move — onto the stretcher, into the aircraft, at the receiving facility — recheck depth and waveform. Many unplanned extubations occur during these transfers.

For children over about two years, the uncuffed tube size is roughly (age ÷ 4) + 4 mm and the cuffed size (age ÷ 4) + 3.5 mm; have a half size above and below ready. Length-based tapes give tube size and drug doses in one step and reduce calculation errors under stress. Depth at the lips is about three times the internal diameter.

Small movements matter: in an infant the trachea may be only 4–5 cm long, so flexion or extension of the head can move the tip from mid-trachea into a main bronchus or out through the cords. Keep the head in a neutral position, tape securely across the upper lip, and recheck depth and capnography after every move and before take-off.
In neonates, the tip-to-lip depth is approximately weight in kilograms + 6 cm. A chest X-ray on arrival confirms the tip sits between the clavicles and the carina.
An intubated patient is moved from the ICU bed to your stretcher, then into the aircraft. On reconnection the waveform is absent and the SpO₂ is still 98 %.

High saturation reassures nobody: a well pre-oxygenated patient can keep a high SpO₂ for minutes after displacement. Loss of the waveform after a move is a displaced or disconnected tube until proven otherwise.

Rigid (Yankauer or large-bore) catheters clear the oropharynx of blood, vomit and particulate matter. Large-bore rigid catheters clear thick material far faster than standard Yankauers. Soft (French) catheters pass through endotracheal and tracheostomy tubes or the nose.

Typical suction pressures are 80–120 mmHg for endotracheal suction in adults (lower in children and neonates, often 60–100 mmHg and 60–80 mmHg respectively); oropharyngeal clearance of heavy contamination may use higher settings. Follow your device and protocol.

Size an endotracheal suction catheter so it occludes no more than about half the internal diameter of the tube; a quick rule is catheter size in French ≈ 2 × the tube size in mm (for example, a 14 Fr catheter for a 7.0 tube). Too large a catheter can evacuate the lungs and cause atelectasis.

Pre-oxygenate with FiO₂ 1.0 for 30–60 seconds. Insert the catheter without suction to the carina or until resistance, withdraw 1 cm, then apply suction while withdrawing with a rotating motion. Limit each pass to about 10–15 seconds in adults (shorter in children). Allow re-oxygenation between passes.

Closed in-line suction systems allow suctioning without disconnecting the ventilator, preserving PEEP and reducing aerosol exposure — preferable in ARDS, high PEEP, and infectious disease. Routine saline instillation is not recommended: it can worsen oxygenation and spread contamination.
Watch for hypoxaemia, bradycardia (vagal stimulation), arrhythmias, raised intracranial pressure, mucosal trauma and bleeding, and bronchospasm.

Massive regurgitation or haemorrhage defeats laryngoscopy and fills the lungs. Position head-up if possible, use a large-bore rigid suction catheter, and lead with it during laryngoscopy (suction-assisted laryngoscopy and airway decontamination, SALAD). After clearing the oropharynx, park the catheter in the upper oesophagus to the left of the blade to control ongoing regurgitation.
After intubation, suction through the tube before ventilating if aspirated material is present; bronchoscopy at the receiving centre may be needed for particulate aspiration.

Check suction at the start of every shift and before every airway: power or battery, canister seated and empty, tubing connected, a rigid catheter and soft catheters of the right sizes, and the vacuum reading with the tubing occluded. Portable units lose strength as batteries drain; a manual hand-powered suction is a useful backup.

Complications are mostly preventable. Hypoxaemia is limited by pre-oxygenation and short passes. Mucosal trauma and bleeding are limited by appropriate pressures, not jabbing the catheter, and stopping 1 cm short of the carina. Atelectasis is limited by catheter size no more than half the tube lumen and by closed systems that preserve PEEP. Infection risk is reduced by sterile technique for endotracheal suction.
Document what you removed — volume, colour, blood or particulate matter — because it informs the receiving team about aspiration, pneumonia or haemorrhage.

Neonates and infants: use lower pressures and smaller catheters, limit each pass to about 5–10 seconds, suction the mouth before the nose (nasal stimulation can trigger a gasp and aspiration of oral contents), and watch for bradycardia. In the newly born, routine deep suction is not recommended; suction only if the airway is obstructed.
Raised intracranial pressure: suctioning causes coughing and surges in ICP. Ensure adequate sedation and analgesia, pre-oxygenate, keep passes short, and avoid repeated passes.
Tracheostomy patients: measure the catheter against the tube length or use pre-measured suction to avoid trauma to the carina. Inner cannulas can be removed and cleaned when secretions are thick.
Infectious disease: closed in-line systems reduce aerosol exposure; wear appropriate PPE for open suction.
An intubated pneumonia patient on a 90-minute flight develops rising peak pressures, a shark-fin capnogram and falling SpO₂. Plateau pressure is unchanged.

A rising peak with an unchanged plateau is a resistance problem; the most likely cause in this patient is secretions in the tube. Dry oxygen and long transport thicken secretions; heat and moisture exchangers help.

Phase I is the inspiratory baseline, near zero, as dead-space gas without CO₂ leaves first. Phase II is the expiratory upstroke as alveolar gas mixes with dead space. Phase III is the alveolar plateau, ending in the end-tidal value (normally 35–45 mmHg). Phase 0 (sometimes called phase IV) is the inspiratory downstroke as fresh gas enters.

EtCO₂ is usually 2–5 mmHg below PaCO₂ in healthy lungs. The gap widens with dead space: low cardiac output, pulmonary embolism, COPD, overdistension, and hypovolaemia. In those patients EtCO₂ underestimates PaCO₂, so trend EtCO₂ against a blood gas.

During CPR, EtCO₂ reflects pulmonary blood flow generated by compressions. A value persistently below about 10 mmHg suggests poor-quality compressions — change compressors, check depth and rate — or a very poor prognosis when it persists after prolonged resuscitation despite good CPR (interpreted alongside other factors, never alone).

A sudden rise in EtCO₂ (often to 35–45 mmHg or more) during compressions is an early sign of return of spontaneous circulation, often before a pulse is palpable. Bicarbonate administration also transiently raises EtCO₂, which must be distinguished from ROSC.
Sedation and opioids: nasal-oral capnography detects hypoventilation and apnoea before oxygen saturation falls, particularly when supplemental oxygen keeps SpO₂ high.
Brain injury: target normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–40). Establish the PaCO₂–EtCO₂ gap with a blood gas, then ventilate to the EtCO₂ that corresponds; hyperventilate only briefly for signs of herniation.
Metabolic acidosis: in a spontaneously breathing patient a very low EtCO₂ reflects respiratory compensation (for example, in DKA); after intubation, preserving that low CO₂ is essential.
Shock: falling EtCO₂ at constant ventilation suggests falling cardiac output.

End-tidal CO₂ depends on three things: production by metabolism, delivery to the lungs by the circulation, and elimination by ventilation. A change in the number always means one of those three has changed — or the equipment has.
Production rises with fever, shivering, seizures, sepsis, malignant hyperthermia, and when bicarbonate is given (it is converted to CO₂). Production falls with hypothermia and deep sedation.

Delivery depends on cardiac output and pulmonary blood flow. A sudden fall at constant ventilation means falling output, a pulmonary embolism or cardiac arrest; a sudden rise during CPR suggests ROSC.

Elimination depends on alveolar ventilation: rate × (tidal volume − dead space). Hypoventilation raises EtCO₂; hyperventilation lowers it. Increased dead space lowers EtCO₂ relative to PaCO₂ even though the arterial value may be rising.
You transport an intubated septic patient. Over the flight, the capnogram tells a story — if you read it.

CPAP applies one continuous pressure throughout the breath. It recruits collapsed alveoli and increases FRC, reducing shunt and improving oxygenation; in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema it reduces preload and LV afterload by raising intrathoracic pressure; it splints open the upper airway in obstructive sleep apnoea; and it offsets auto-PEEP, reducing the work of triggering in COPD.

BiPAP (bilevel) adds a higher inspiratory pressure (IPAP) above the expiratory pressure (EPAP, equivalent to PEEP). The difference, the pressure support, augments tidal volume and so improves ventilation and CO₂ clearance — the key indication being hypercapnic COPD exacerbation.

Strong evidence supports NIV in acute hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (pH roughly 7.25–7.35) and cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It is also used for pre-oxygenation, in immunocompromised patients with respiratory failure, and in selected asthma and pneumonia patients with close monitoring.

Contraindications: respiratory or cardiac arrest, inability to protect the airway or clear secretions, severely depressed consciousness (except hypercapnic narcosis expected to improve quickly), vomiting or upper GI bleeding, facial trauma or burns preventing a seal, recent upper airway or oesophageal surgery, untreated pneumothorax, and haemodynamic instability (positive pressure lowers venous return).

Reassess within 30–60 minutes and continuously in transport: respiratory rate, work of breathing, SpO₂, EtCO₂ trend, mental status, leak, synchrony and blood pressure. Expected improvement: falling respiratory rate and heart rate, better comfort, improving pH and CO₂.

Failure signs: worsening mental status, inability to tolerate the mask, rising CO₂ or falling pH, persistent tachypnoea, haemodynamic instability, vomiting. Delayed intubation after failed NIV is associated with worse outcomes; in transport, where intubating mid-flight is difficult, the threshold to intubate before departure should be lower if improvement is not clear.
Altitude: mask leak and gastric distension may increase; some transport devices compensate for altitude. Communication is harder under a mask; agree hand signals.

Heated, humidified high-flow nasal oxygen (often 30–60 L/min) delivers a reliable FiO₂, washes CO₂ from the anatomical dead space, produces a small positive pressure, and is comfortable. It is useful in hypoxaemic respiratory failure, for pre-oxygenation and for apnoeic oxygenation. It is oxygen-hungry, which matters for transport oxygen calculations.

The interface decides whether NIV works. Oronasal (full-face) masks suit acute respiratory failure because breathless patients breathe through the mouth. Nasal masks suit calmer patients and allow speech. Total-face masks and helmets spread pressure over a larger area and help when pressure sores or claustrophobia limit other masks.

Fit the mask so it seals without excessive strap tension: one or two fingers should slide under the straps. Small leaks are tolerated by ventilators designed for NIV; large leaks cause asynchrony, failure to trigger or cycle, and dry eyes. Re-fit rather than tighten.

Watch the patient breathe with the machine. Triggering delays, double triggering or breaths that end before the patient finishes inhaling increase work of breathing. Adjust the trigger sensitivity and rise time, coach the patient, and consider low-dose anxiolysis — while never sedating a patient so deeply that airway protection is lost.
Gastric distension, eye irritation, nasal bridge pressure injury and aspiration are the common complications; a gastric tube may be needed on long transports.
A 72-year-old with hypertension is sitting bolt upright, frothy sputum, SpO₂ 82 % on a non-rebreather, BP 210/120, HR 118, crackles to the apices. She is alert and frightened.

Sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary oedema: high afterload drives fluid into the lungs. CPAP or BiPAP lowers preload and afterload and recruits flooded alveoli, while high-dose nitrates lower afterload. Intubation can often be avoided.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is insulin deficiency with counter-regulatory hormone excess: glucose usually above 250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L), a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.30, bicarbonate < 18), and ketones. Kussmaul breathing compensates for the acidosis. Osmotic diuresis causes profound dehydration — often 5–8 litres in adults — and total-body potassium depletion even when the plasma potassium reads high.

The hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) is seen more in older type 2 diabetics: glucose often above 600 mg/dL (33 mmol/L), serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, little or no ketosis or acidosis, and greater dehydration (often 8–10 litres). Altered consciousness tracks osmolality. Mortality is higher than DKA, partly from age, comorbidity and thrombosis.

Order of treatment for both: fluids first (isotonic crystalloid to restore circulation), then potassium (check before insulin; replace if low — many protocols withhold insulin until K⁺ is at least 3.3 mmol/L), then insulin as a fixed-rate infusion. Add dextrose as glucose falls so insulin can continue until ketones clear. Bicarbonate is reserved for extreme acidaemia per protocol. In HHS, lower glucose and sodium more slowly to avoid cerebral oedema.

Intubation is dangerous: the patient is compensating for a severe metabolic acidosis with a very high minute ventilation. Apnoea and then "normal" ventilator settings can drop the pH precipitously and cause arrest. Avoid intubation unless the airway is truly threatened; if needed, keep apnoea short and set a minute ventilation that matches the patient's own.

Potassium falls as insulin and fluids act; hypokalaemia causes arrhythmias. Monitor the ECG continuously and recheck potassium on long transports. In children, rapid fluid shifts risk cerebral oedema — watch for headache, falling GCS, bradycardia and hypertension, and treat with hyperosmolar therapy.

Hypoglycaemia (glucose below about 70 mg/dL, with symptoms; severe when the patient needs assistance) causes sweating, tremor and tachycardia from adrenergic response, then confusion, seizures and coma from neuroglycopenia. Beta-blockers mask the adrenergic warning signs. Sulfonylurea overdose causes prolonged, recurrent hypoglycaemia; octreotide reduces insulin release in that setting.

Treat with IV dextrose (for example D10 in titrated boluses, or D50 in adults per protocol), or IM glucagon if no access (less effective in depleted glycogen stores — alcoholics, starvation). Recheck glucose frequently and follow with food or a dextrose infusion.

Thyroid storm is life-threatening thyrotoxicosis: fever, tachycardia (often atrial fibrillation), agitation or delirium, vomiting, diarrhoea and high-output heart failure, often precipitated by infection, surgery, trauma or stopping antithyroid drugs. Treat in sequence: a beta-blocker (propranolol is classic; esmolol when titration is needed) for adrenergic effects, a thionamide (propylthiouracil or methimazole) to block synthesis, iodine at least an hour after the thionamide to block release, corticosteroids, cooling and supportive care. Avoid aspirin for fever (it displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins).

Myxoedema coma is decompensated hypothyroidism: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation with hypercapnia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia and depressed consciousness, often in an older woman in winter. Treat with IV levothyroxine (often with liothyronine per specialist advice), stress-dose hydrocortisone until adrenal insufficiency is excluded, passive rewarming, ventilatory support and careful correction of sodium. These patients are very sensitive to sedatives.
A 16-year-old with type 1 diabetes, vomiting for a day: GCS 13, RR 36 deep, HR 130, BP 98/60, glucose 540 mg/dL, pH 7.04, HCO₃⁻ 5, K⁺ 5.6, Na⁺ 131. A 90-minute flight to a paediatric ICU.

The adrenal cortex makes cortisol (glucocorticoid), aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) and androgens. Cortisol supports blood pressure by sensitising vessels to catecholamines, raises glucose and modulates inflammation; aldosterone retains sodium and excretes potassium. The adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine.

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease: autoimmune, infection, haemorrhage) loses both cortisol and aldosterone, so hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hyperpigmentation are typical. Secondary insufficiency (pituitary disease, or suppression by long-term steroid therapy — the commonest cause) loses cortisol but aldosterone is largely preserved, so potassium is usually normal.

Adrenal crisis is shock that responds poorly to fluids and vasopressors, often with abdominal pain, vomiting, confusion, fever, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. It is precipitated by infection, trauma, surgery, vomiting that prevents oral steroids, or abrupt withdrawal of chronic steroid therapy. Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcal sepsis.

Treat immediately: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM in adults (about 50–100 mg/m², often 2 mg/kg up to 100 mg in children per local protocol), isotonic fluids with dextrose if hypoglycaemic, and treatment of the precipitant. Do not delay hydrocortisone for a cortisol level. At doses of 100 mg and above, hydrocortisone provides enough mineralocorticoid effect that fludrocortisone is not needed acutely.

Patients on long-term steroids (for example prednisone 5 mg or more daily for more than a few weeks) may not mount a stress response. Many carry an emergency card and an injection kit; ask about it, and give stress-dose hydrocortisone in serious illness or injury.

In septic shock needing ongoing or escalating vasopressor therapy, guidelines suggest IV hydrocortisone (commonly 200 mg/day in divided doses or infusion). Trials show faster shock reversal; mortality benefit is inconsistent. Etomidate's transient adrenal suppression after a single induction dose is debated; many clinicians simply ensure hydrocortisone is considered in refractory shock regardless of induction agent.

A catecholamine-secreting tumour can cause paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and palpitations, and crises with severe hypertension, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy and pulmonary oedema — sometimes triggered by anaesthesia, trauma, steroids or certain drugs (metoclopramide, some antidepressants).

Treat with alpha-blockade or vasodilators first (phentolamine, nicardipine, nitroprusside per protocol). Never give a beta-blocker alone: blocking beta-2 mediated vasodilation leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and blood pressure can rise further. Beta-blockers are added only after adequate alpha-blockade, to control tachycardia.

A 62-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis on long-term prednisone, two days after bowel surgery, vomiting for 24 hours: BP 76/40 despite 3 L of fluid and norepinephrine 0.3 mcg/kg/min, HR 118, glucose 58 mg/dL, Na⁺ 129, K⁺ 4.6.

Anyone taking the equivalent of prednisone 5 mg a day or more for longer than about three to four weeks in the past year may have a suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis. So may patients using high-dose inhaled or topical steroids, those with known Addison's disease or pituitary disease, and those recently given etomidate repeatedly. In serious illness, trauma, or before surgery they need stress-dose steroids.

Practical doses in transport: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM for crisis or serious illness, followed in hospital by 200 mg per day (by infusion or divided doses). Children receive weight- or body-surface-based doses per protocol. Many patients carry an emergency card and a hydrocortisone injection kit; use the patient's own supply if needed and record the time given.

Clues that a shocked patient may have adrenal insufficiency: poor response to fluids and vasopressors, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (primary), eosinophilia, vomiting and abdominal pain, a history of steroid use, or hyperpigmentation. When in doubt in refractory shock, hydrocortisone is low-risk and potentially life-saving.

AKI is a rapid rise in creatinine or fall in urine output (for example, creatinine rising by 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, or urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours). Classify by cause. Pre-renal: reduced perfusion from hypovolaemia, shock, heart failure or renal artery disease; the kidney itself is initially normal and recovers with perfusion. Intrinsic: acute tubular necrosis from prolonged ischaemia or toxins (contrast, aminoglycosides, myoglobin), glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis. Post-renal: obstruction of both outflows (or one in a single kidney) — prostate, stones, tumours, a blocked catheter.

In transport, the reversible causes are what you can act on: restore perfusion pressure, stop nephrotoxins, and relieve obstruction (a urinary catheter, or flushing a blocked one). Track urine output hourly in critically ill patients.

Potassium above about 6.5 mmol/L, or any hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, is an emergency. The ECG progresses roughly from peaked T waves, to PR prolongation and flattened P waves, to QRS widening, to a sine wave and then ventricular fibrillation or asystole — but the sequence is unreliable and arrest can occur without warning.

Stabilise the membrane with IV calcium (calcium gluconate 3 g or calcium chloride 1 g in adults, typically, repeated if ECG changes persist); it acts within minutes, lasts 30–60 minutes and does not lower potassium. Shift potassium into cells with insulin plus dextrose (for example 10 units regular insulin with 25 g dextrose) and nebulised salbutamol; bicarbonate helps mainly in concurrent acidosis. Remove potassium with dialysis (definitive in renal failure), potassium binders, or loop diuretics if the kidneys work. Recheck glucose after insulin.

Muscle breakdown from crush, prolonged immobilisation, exertion, seizures, hyperthermia or drugs releases myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase. Myoglobin causes tubular injury, especially in hypovolaemia and acidosis. Dark urine with a dipstick positive for blood but few red cells suggests myoglobinuria.

Treat with early, aggressive isotonic fluids to maintain a high urine output (often targeted around 200–300 mL/h in adults per protocol), correct hyperkalaemia, and in crush injury start fluids before release where possible to blunt reperfusion hyperkalaemia and acidosis. Avoid succinylcholine.

Ask when the last dialysis was. Missed dialysis brings hyperkalaemia, fluid overload with pulmonary oedema, metabolic acidosis and uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding from platelet dysfunction).

Protect the access: avoid blood pressure cuffs, IVs and venepuncture on an arm with a fistula or graft. A palpable thrill and audible bruit indicate patency. Bleeding from a fistula can be torrential; apply firm direct pressure. Central dialysis catheters should not be used for routine access except in an emergency by protocol, as they are often locked with concentrated heparin or citrate that must be aspirated first.

Drug choice: avoid succinylcholine if potassium is unknown or high; use rocuronium. Many drugs accumulate (morphine metabolites, some antibiotics); fentanyl is preferred to morphine. Fluid overload is better treated with nitrates and NIV than with fluid restriction alone; diuretics may be ineffective in anuric patients.
A construction worker trapped under a collapsed wall for five hours. Legs swollen and tense, HR 118, BP 104/66. Extrication is imminent.

Plasma sodium sets cell volume, and the brain has no room to swell. Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia — seizures, coma, vomiting with confusion — is treated with hypertonic saline boluses (commonly 3 % saline, 100–150 mL over 10–20 minutes, repeated up to two or three times) aiming to raise sodium by 4–6 mmol/L, which is usually enough to stop symptoms.

Chronic hyponatraemia (present more than 48 hours, or of unknown duration) must not be corrected too fast: limit the rise to about 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours (lower in high-risk patients such as alcoholics, the malnourished and those with hypokalaemia) to avoid osmotic demyelination, which appears days later with dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis.

Hypernatraemia reflects water deficit — elderly or disabled patients without access to water, diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis. Correct gradually with hypotonic fluids, lowering sodium by no more than about 10–12 mmol/L per day in chronic cases, to avoid cerebral oedema.

Hypocalcaemia causes perioral and digital paraesthesia, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, seizures, QT prolongation and hypotension. Causes include massive transfusion (citrate binds calcium), pancreatitis, hypoparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia. Treat symptomatic patients with IV calcium (gluconate peripherally; chloride contains about three times the elemental calcium and is irritating, so is preferred centrally). In major haemorrhage, give calcium early and often.

Hypercalcaemia ("stones, bones, groans and psychiatric overtones") causes dehydration, confusion, short QT and arrhythmias, usually from malignancy or hyperparathyroidism. Treat with isotonic fluids first; bisphosphonates and calcitonin follow in hospital.

Magnesium below normal predisposes to torsades de pointes, refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV is given for torsades, severe asthma and eclampsia. Hypermagnesaemia (often iatrogenic in pre-eclampsia treatment or renal failure) causes loss of deep tendon reflexes, then respiratory depression and heart block; calcium is the antidote.

One: is the pH acidaemic (< 7.35) or alkalaemic (> 7.45)? Two: which value explains it — PaCO₂ (respiratory) or HCO₃⁻ (metabolic)? Three: is compensation appropriate? For metabolic acidosis, expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (± 2), Winter's formula; acute respiratory acidosis raises HCO₃⁻ about 1 per 10 mmHg CO₂, chronic about 4. Four: for metabolic acidosis calculate the anion gap, Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normal about 8–12. Five: in a high-gap acidosis, compare the change in gap with the change in bicarbonate to uncover a hidden second metabolic disorder.

High anion-gap causes include lactate, ketones (diabetic, alcoholic, starvation), renal failure, and toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, iron, isoniazid). Normal-gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis follows diarrhoea, large volumes of saline and renal tubular acidosis.

Heat stroke is a core temperature above about 40 °C with central nervous system dysfunction. It kills by multi-organ failure; the treatment is rapid cooling — cold-water immersion is fastest for exertional heat stroke, or evaporative cooling with mist and fans plus ice packs. Antipyretics do not work. Stop cooling around 38.5–39 °C to avoid overshoot.

Hypothermia is graded by core temperature (mild 32–35 °C, moderate 28–32 °C, severe below 28 °C) and by clinical signs. Handle severely hypothermic patients gently and horizontally to avoid triggering ventricular fibrillation; the cold heart may resist defibrillation and drugs until rewarmed. Rewarm actively; "not dead until warm and dead" applies, and ECMO centres can rewarm patients in arrest.

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (Sepsis-3). Organ dysfunction is identified by a rise in the SOFA score of two or more points. qSOFA — respiratory rate ≥ 22, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤ 100 — flags patients at higher risk of death but is not recommended as a single screening tool.

Septic shock is sepsis with persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg and a serum lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation. Mortality is substantially higher than sepsis alone.

Measure lactate (and remeasure if above 2). Take blood cultures before antibiotics when this causes no meaningful delay. Give broad-spectrum antibiotics as soon as possible — within one hour for probable septic shock; delays raise mortality. Give 30 mL/kg of crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4, guided by reassessment of perfusion and fluid responsiveness rather than as a fixed target. Start a vasopressor if MAP remains below 65 during or after fluids.

Balanced crystalloids (lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte) are suggested over saline for large volumes. Albumin may be considered when large volumes of crystalloid are needed. Starch solutions are avoided.

Aim for MAP ≥ 65 mmHg initially, adjusted for chronic hypertension. Track perfusion, not just pressure: mental status, capillary refill, skin mottling, urine output (≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h) and lactate clearance. Capillary refill time is a validated, simple target.

Before giving more fluid, ask whether the patient is fluid-responsive (passive leg raise with a change in stroke volume or pulse pressure, pulse-pressure variation in a ventilated patient) and whether lungs and oxygenation will tolerate it. Over-resuscitation causes pulmonary oedema, abdominal compartment syndrome and worse outcomes.

Hydrocortisone (commonly 200 mg/day) is suggested when vasopressor needs are ongoing. Source control — draining an abscess, removing an infected line, relieving obstructed infected urine — must happen as soon as practical; transport to a centre that can do it is part of treatment.

Transport is not a pause in sepsis care. Make sure the first antibiotic dose has been given and note the time; if the flight is long and a second dose falls due, carry it. Keep fluids and vasopressors on pumps, and bring enough of each for the flight plus a reserve.

Reassess perfusion at regular intervals: MAP, heart rate, mental status, capillary refill and, where measured, urine output and lactate. Escalate norepinephrine and add vasopressin per protocol if MAP falls; consider hydrocortisone for escalating requirements.

Hand over the timeline clearly: when sepsis was recognised, cultures taken, antibiotics given, the fluid volume received, the vasopressor course, and the suspected source with any source-control plan.

Older adults may present with confusion, falls or hypothermia rather than fever. Immunocompromised patients — chemotherapy, transplant, high-dose steroids — may have few signs; neutropenic fever is treated as an emergency with immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics. Pregnant women have physiologically higher heart rates and lower blood pressures, which can mask early sepsis; obstetric sources (endometritis, chorioamnionitis) are common.

Children compensate with tachycardia and vasoconstriction; hypotension appears late. Paediatric fluid boluses are 10–20 mL/kg with reassessment after each, and epinephrine or norepinephrine is chosen by clinical phenotype (cold versus warm shock). Neonates may show apnoea, poor feeding or temperature instability.
Asplenic patients are at risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection with encapsulated organisms; they deteriorate rapidly and need immediate antibiotics.

Standard precautions apply to every patient: hand hygiene, gloves for body fluids, eye protection when splashes are likely, safe sharps handling. Contact precautions (gown and gloves) add protection against organisms spread by touch, such as MRSA and Clostridioides difficile (soap and water for hands — alcohol does not kill spores). Droplet precautions (surgical mask within close range) cover influenza, pertussis and meningococcus. Airborne precautions (fit-tested N95 or equivalent respirator) cover tuberculosis, measles and varicella, and aerosol-generating procedures in respiratory viral illness.

Aircraft cabins are small and air circulation varies by airframe. Put a mask on the patient when possible, use HEPA filters on ventilator and BVM circuits, minimise aerosol-generating procedures in flight (secure the airway before departure, use closed suction), and clean the aircraft per protocol afterwards. Some programmes decline or modify transport of high-consequence infections without special containment.

Bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered mental status, though all four are present in a minority. A petechial or purpuric rash suggests meningococcal disease, which can progress to septic shock and purpura fulminans within hours. Infants may show only irritability, poor feeding, a bulging fontanelle or hypothermia.

Give antibiotics without delay — do not wait for lumbar puncture or imaging when transport or testing will delay treatment. Dexamethasone given with or just before the first antibiotic dose reduces neurological sequelae in some forms (notably pneumococcal). Use droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective therapy; close contacts of meningococcal disease, including crew exposed to respiratory secretions without protection (such as during intubation), need prophylaxis.

Necrotising soft-tissue infection causes pain out of proportion to the findings, rapidly spreading erythema, tense oedema, crepitus, bullae and systemic toxicity. It is a surgical emergency: antibiotics, resuscitation and urgent debridement. Transport to a surgical centre should not wait for imaging.

Toxic shock syndrome (staphylococcal or streptococcal) produces fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension and multi-organ involvement; look for retained tampons, wounds or surgical sites. Treat as septic shock, remove the source, and add an antibiotic that suppresses toxin production per protocol.

For a needlestick or mucosal splash: wash with soap and water (irrigate mucosa), report immediately, and arrange evaluation of the source and the exposed worker. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is most effective started within hours, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72 hours. Hepatitis B vaccination status determines further management; there is no prophylaxis for hepatitis C, but follow-up testing is needed.
Programmes should have a clear post-exposure process available 24 hours a day, including for exposures far from base.
A 19-year-old student: fever, headache, confusion, BP 84/46, a non-blanching purpuric rash spreading on the legs.

After a transport, clean all surfaces the patient or crew touched with a hospital-grade disinfectant, respecting the product's contact time. For C. difficile and other spore-forming organisms, use a sporicidal (bleach-based) product. Single-use items go to clinical waste; reusable equipment (laryngoscope handles, monitor cables, stretcher mattresses) follows the manufacturer's decontamination process.

For airborne pathogens, the aircraft's air exchange rate determines how long to leave doors open or ventilation running before the next patient; follow programme policy. Crew should remove PPE in a defined order to avoid self-contamination — usually gloves first, then gown, then eye protection, then respirator, with hand hygiene between steps.
Document exposures and decontamination steps. A clear process protects the next patient and the crew.

A toxidrome is a pattern of signs that points to a class of poison. Look at heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, respiratory rate, pupils, skin (dry or sweaty), bowel sounds and mental status. Mixed ingestions blur the picture, so treat the patient in front of you.

Sympathomimetic (cocaine, amphetamines): agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils, sweating. Treat with benzodiazepines, cooling and avoidance of physical restraint struggles. Anticholinergic (diphenhydramine, tricyclics, jimson weed): "hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter" — tachycardia, hyperthermia, dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, urinary retention, delirium; physostigmine has a role in pure anticholinergic delirium under expert guidance.

Cholinergic (organophosphates, nerve agents): SLUDGE/DUMBELS — salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis, plus bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm ("the killer Bs") and bradycardia, with miosis. Treat with large, repeated doses of atropine titrated to drying of secretions, and pralidoxime for organophosphates; decontaminate and protect the crew. Opioid: miosis, respiratory depression and coma; naloxone titrated to breathing, not wakefulness. Sedative-hypnotic: depressed consciousness with relatively normal vital signs; support the airway and breathing.

Salicylates: tinnitus, vomiting, hyperthermia, tachypnoea, a mixed respiratory alkalosis and high-gap metabolic acidosis, and altered mental status. The patient survives by hyperventilating; if intubated, the minute ventilation must stay high or the pH falls, salicylate enters the brain and the patient may arrest. Alkalinise with sodium bicarbonate, give dextrose for neuroglycopenia, and arrange haemodialysis for severe toxicity. Methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) is highly concentrated and has a distinctive smell.

Tricyclic antidepressants: anticholinergic signs, seizures, hypotension and sodium-channel blockade with a wide QRS (> 100 ms) and a tall terminal R in aVR. Treat QRS widening, hypotension or arrhythmia with sodium bicarbonate boluses (1–2 mEq/kg, repeated) to a pH of about 7.45–7.55; avoid type IA and IC antiarrhythmics.

Calcium-channel and beta-blockers: bradycardia and hypotension, with hyperglycaemia typical of calcium-channel blockers. Treat with fluids, calcium, glucagon (beta-blockers), vasopressors, and high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy (insulin around 1 unit/kg bolus then infusion with dextrose and potassium monitoring) per toxicology advice; lipid emulsion for refractory lipophilic drug toxicity.

Acetaminophen: few early symptoms, then liver injury at 24–72 hours. N-acetylcysteine is most effective within 8 hours of ingestion; never withhold it while waiting for levels if presentation is late or the dose is unknown.

Toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol): inebriation, then a high anion-gap acidosis with a raised osmolar gap; methanol causes visual loss, ethylene glycol renal failure. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase; dialysis removes the parent compound and toxic metabolites.

Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 200–250 times more avidly than oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve left, so tissues receive less oxygen. Headache, nausea, confusion and syncope are common; standard pulse oximetry reads falsely normal because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin. Give 100 % oxygen (the half-life of COHb falls from about 4–6 hours on air to about 60–90 minutes on 100 %); hyperbaric oxygen is considered for severe cases, pregnancy, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits.

Cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase, halting aerobic metabolism: sudden collapse, seizures, severe lactic acidosis and a high venous oxygen saturation. House fires (burning plastics) cause combined CO and cyanide poisoning; consider cyanide in smoke-inhalation victims with altered consciousness, hypotension or lactate above about 8 mmol/L. Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin and turns skin and urine red, interfering with some lab tests.

Airway, breathing and circulation first; check glucose in every altered patient. Decontaminate before transport when the poison is on the skin or clothing (organophosphates, chemicals) to protect the crew and aircraft. Activated charcoal is considered only when the airway is protected and within about an hour of a significant ingestion of an adsorbable toxin; it does not bind iron, lithium, alcohols or metals.
Seizures from poisoning are treated with benzodiazepines first; phenytoin is ineffective and harmful in some (tricyclics). Contact a poison centre early; transport time is a good time to call.

Packed red blood cells (PRBCs) restore oxygen-carrying capacity; one unit raises haemoglobin by about 1 g/dL in an adult. Plasma (fresh frozen or liquid/thawed) replaces clotting factors. Platelets (one apheresis unit raises the count by roughly 30,000–50,000/µL) treat thrombocytopenia or dysfunction. Cryoprecipitate is concentrated fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII. Low-titre O whole blood provides all components in one bag and is increasingly carried by prehospital services.

Universal donors: O-negative red cells (O-positive acceptable for most males and for women beyond childbearing age when stocks require); AB plasma is the universal plasma donor (low-titre A plasma is used by some programmes). Women of childbearing potential receive O-negative red cells when the type is unknown to avoid Rh sensitisation.

Massive transfusion is commonly defined as 10 or more units of red cells in 24 hours, or a rapid rate such as 3–4 units in an hour. Damage-control resuscitation gives products in a balanced ratio approximating whole blood — about 1:1:1 plasma, platelets and red cells — limits crystalloid, permits low blood pressure until haemorrhage control (except in head injury), and treats coagulopathy early with tranexamic acid (within 3 hours of injury) and fibrinogen replacement guided by testing.

Hazards rise with volume: hypocalcaemia (citrate binds calcium — give calcium early), hypothermia (warm every product; cold blood worsens coagulopathy), hyperkalaemia (stored cells leak potassium), acidosis, dilutional coagulopathy, and transfusion-associated circulatory overload.

Watch closely during the first 15 minutes of each unit and throughout. If a reaction is suspected: stop the transfusion, keep the line open with saline, check the patient's identity against the unit, treat the symptoms, and report and return the bag per protocol.

Acute haemolytic reaction (ABO incompatibility, usually clerical error): fever, chills, back or flank pain, hypotension, haemoglobinuria and DIC — can be fatal; stop, fluids, support. Febrile non-haemolytic: fever and chills without other signs; antipyretics after excluding haemolysis. Allergic: urticaria and itching; antihistamines; anaphylaxis (wheeze, hypotension) needs adrenaline. TRALI: acute hypoxaemia and bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours, often with hypotension and fever; supportive ventilation. TACO: hypertension, pulmonary oedema and volume overload; slow or stop, diuretics, NIV. Sepsis from contaminated product: high fever and shock, especially with platelets.
A 28-year-old motorcyclist with a pelvic fracture and femur fracture: HR 140, BP 74/40, cool and pale. You carry 2 units of low-titre O whole blood and 2 units of plasma.

Blood is stored in validated coolers that hold 1–6 °C for a defined time; record the temperature and time out of storage, and return unused units per protocol. Inspect each unit for leaks, clots or discolouration, and check the label and expiry. Two-person verification of patient identity is the main defence against ABO-incompatible transfusion, even in emergencies.

Use a filtered blood administration set, a fluid warmer for rapid transfusion, and a pressure infuser for haemorrhage. Do not run blood with dextrose or lactated Ringer's in the same line unless the protocol permits — calcium in LR can clot citrated blood, and dextrose can haemolyse cells. Normal saline is compatible.
Document unit numbers, start and stop times, volumes and any reaction. Blood products are traceable to donors; good records protect patients.

Upper GI bleeding (above the ligament of Treitz) presents with haematemesis, coffee-ground vomit or melaena; common causes are peptic ulcer, varices, Mallory–Weiss tears and oesophagitis. Brisk upper bleeding can also cause haematochezia. Lower GI bleeding usually presents with fresh blood per rectum (diverticulosis, angiodysplasia, colitis).

Resuscitate with blood products guided by haemodynamics and a restrictive transfusion threshold (around Hb 7 g/dL) in stable patients without cardiac disease; massive bleeding needs balanced products. Reverse anticoagulants as indicated. A proton-pump inhibitor is commonly started for suspected upper bleeding. Large-bore access, suction and a plan for the airway are essential: blood in the airway turns intubation into a contaminated, high-risk procedure.

Patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension bleed from oesophageal or gastric varices. Treatment adds octreotide (splanchnic vasoconstrictor) and prophylactic antibiotics (they reduce infection and rebleeding and improve survival) to resuscitation, with endoscopic banding as definitive therapy. Avoid over-transfusion, which raises portal pressure. In uncontrolled bleeding, a balloon tamponade device (Sengstaken–Blakemore or Minnesota tube) is a bridge, placed only after intubation.

Cirrhotic patients have a complex coagulopathy (both bleeding and clotting tendencies), thrombocytopenia, encephalopathy (lactulose; look for precipitants such as bleeding and infection), ascites with possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatorenal syndrome and relative hypotension. Acute liver failure (for example from acetaminophen) adds cerebral oedema and hypoglycaemia.

Acute pancreatitis (gallstones and alcohol are commonest) causes epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting and raised lipase. Severe disease brings systemic inflammation, third-spacing, hypocalcaemia, ARDS and shock. Give goal-directed fluids — avoid both under- and over-resuscitation — analgesia, and organ support.

Bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation; decompress with a gastric tube, replace fluids and electrolytes, and watch for strangulation (constant pain, fever, peritonism, lactate). Perforation causes sudden severe pain, peritonitis and free air; treat with resuscitation, antibiotics and surgery.

Acute mesenteric ischaemia — often an embolus in a patient with atrial fibrillation — causes pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen. Lactate may be normal early. It needs urgent CT angiography and revascularisation; delay costs bowel.

Gas expands at altitude (Boyle's law): an obstructed or distended bowel enlarges, increasing pain, vomiting and splinting of the diaphragm. Decompress with a gastric tube before flight in obstruction or ileus, and vent it during flight. Consider lower cabin altitude when possible.

For a patient vomiting blood with a decreased level of consciousness, the airway decision is about aspiration risk and the transport environment: intubation on the ground with SALAD technique and resuscitation first is usually safer than an airway crisis in flight.

The Glasgow–Blatchford score uses BUN, haemoglobin, systolic pressure, pulse, melaena, syncope, liver disease and heart failure to estimate the need for intervention in upper GI bleeding; a score of zero or one identifies very low-risk patients, while high scores indicate need for urgent endoscopy and possibly transfusion. You will not usually calculate it in flight, but its components are the same red flags you assess.

Destination matters: active haemorrhage needs a centre with immediate endoscopy, interventional radiology and surgery. Variceal bleeding may need TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) capability. Pre-alert early so the receiving team can prepare blood and procedures.
An 81-year-old on apixaban for atrial fibrillation, three episodes of melaena, light-headed: HR 108 (on a beta-blocker), BP 96/58, Hb 7.9, BUN 58, creatinine 1.1.

Reference ranges vary slightly between laboratories, but exam questions and bedside decisions rest on a core set. Learn the units your system uses; US labs report glucose in mg/dL and many others in mmol/L (divide mg/dL by 18).

Haemoglobin is a concentration. In acute haemorrhage it stays near normal until fluid shifts in or crystalloid is given, so a normal first haemoglobin does not exclude major bleeding. Conversely, dilution after crystalloid can lower it without further bleeding.

White cell counts rise with infection, stress, steroids and epinephrine. A low count in sepsis is ominous. Thrombocytopenia has many causes: consumption (DIC, massive bleeding), sequestration (splenomegaly), destruction (immune, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) and dilution.

PT/INR tests the extrinsic and common pathways (factor VII and vitamin K–dependent factors: warfarin, liver disease); aPTT tests the intrinsic and common pathways (heparin, haemophilia). DIC prolongs both, lowers platelets and fibrinogen and raises D-dimer. Viscoelastic tests (TEG, ROTEM) guide targeted product replacement in haemorrhage where available.

Creatinine reflects filtration but rises late; a normal value does not mean normal function in an elderly, small or malnourished patient. A BUN-to-creatinine ratio above about 20 suggests pre-renal states or blood digested from an upper GI bleed.

Troponin rises within hours of myocardial injury; high-sensitivity assays detect smaller injuries earlier, and serial values distinguish acute injury (a rise and/or fall) from chronic elevation (renal failure, heart failure). Troponin elevation is not the same as myocardial infarction: sepsis, pulmonary embolism, myocarditis and tachyarrhythmia also cause it. BNP rises with ventricular stretch and supports a diagnosis of heart failure; it is higher with renal failure and lower in obesity.

Liver tests: AST and ALT rise with hepatocellular injury (ischaemic "shock liver" and acetaminophen produce very high values); bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase rise with obstruction. Ammonia rises in liver failure but does not correlate tightly with encephalopathy severity.

Ask what process could produce all the abnormalities at once. A low bicarbonate, high anion gap, high glucose and high potassium tell the story of DKA. Low platelets, low fibrinogen and prolonged clotting times after major trauma tell the story of consumptive coagulopathy. Low sodium with seizures in a marathon runner tells the story of exercise-associated hyponatraemia.

Arterial samples judge oxygenation and acid–base; venous samples are adequate for pH, bicarbonate, lactate and electrolytes in most stable patients (venous pH about 0.03 lower, PCO₂ about 5 mmHg higher). Venous PO₂ does not measure lung oxygenation.

Calculate the P/F ratio (PaO₂ ÷ FiO₂) to grade hypoxaemia: below 300 indicates impaired oxygenation, and in ARDS, 200–300 is mild, 100–200 moderate and below 100 severe. Calculate the A–a gradient (PAO₂ − PaO₂; normal roughly age/4 + 4 on room air) to separate hypoventilation (normal gradient) from lung disease (widened gradient).

Base excess (normal −2 to +2) summarises the metabolic component; a large negative base deficit in trauma reflects shock and predicts transfusion needs. Point-of-care analysers give results in minutes and are increasingly carried by transport teams.

Begin with what threatens life in the next few minutes: airway patency and protection, breathing and oxygenation, circulation and haemorrhage, disability (GCS, pupils, glucose), and exposure (temperature, rashes, wounds, lines). In medical patients, catastrophic haemorrhage is less common but GI and obstetric bleeding are not.

At an inter-facility transfer, take a structured handover from the sending team (for example SBAR or a programme-specific format), then assess the patient yourself before leaving. Reconcile infusions, ventilator settings, lines and drains against what you were told. Many transport adverse events trace to unreconciled information.

Blood pressure is a late and imperfect marker. Assess end-organ perfusion: mental status, capillary refill (more than about 3 seconds is abnormal in adults), skin temperature and mottling, urine output, and lactate trends. A shock index (heart rate ÷ systolic BP) above about 0.9–1.0 suggests significant shock even with a "normal" pressure.

Classify shock to choose treatment: hypovolaemic (low filling, low output), cardiogenic (high filling, low output), obstructive (tamponade, tension pneumothorax, PE: high filling, low output, obstructed), distributive (low SVR: sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic). Mixed states are common.

Focused ultrasound answers specific questions quickly. RUSH-style protocols look at the pump (pericardial effusion, gross LV function, RV dilation), the tank (IVC size and collapsibility, FAST for free fluid, pleural effusions) and the pipes (aortic aneurysm, DVT). Lung ultrasound identifies pneumothorax (absent sliding, lung point), interstitial syndrome (B-lines) and consolidation.

Ultrasound findings support decisions; they do not replace clinical judgement. IVC size is unreliable in ventilated patients and those with raised intra-abdominal pressure. In flight, vibration and limited space make scanning harder; scan before departure when possible.

A focused history (SAMPLE or OPQRST for pain) and a head-to-toe examination follow stabilisation. In medical transports, the medication list is a diagnostic tool: anticoagulants, beta-blockers masking tachycardia, steroids (adrenal suppression), insulin and sulfonylureas, recent antibiotics.
Reassess after every intervention and at regular intervals in flight. Trends — a rising heart rate, falling EtCO₂, widening pulse pressure — often warn before absolute values cross thresholds.
A 59-year-old found confused at home: BP 80/50, HR 124, RR 28, SpO₂ 92 %, warm extremities, temperature 38.9 °C, lactate 4.8. A 25-minute flight.

In altered patients, document the GCS by component (eye, verbal, motor), pupil size and reactivity, and lateralising signs. A falling motor score is the most important trend. Check glucose early in every altered patient.

The abdomen in critical illness: distension, peritonism, a pulsatile mass, flank bruising (retroperitoneal haemorrhage) and bladder size. A distended abdomen with rising airway pressures and falling urine output suggests abdominal compartment syndrome; bladder pressure above about 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction confirms it.

Match the drug to the problem. Low SVR (distributive shock): norepinephrine first (α-1 with some β-1), vasopressin as a second agent. Poor contractility (cardiogenic shock): an inotrope — dobutamine (β-1 with some β-2 vasodilation) or milrinone (a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor; vasodilating, renally cleared) — usually with norepinephrine to support pressure. Bradycardia with hypotension: epinephrine or dopamine infusions, or pacing.

Epinephrine combines inotropy and vasoconstriction; it raises lactate and heart rate. Phenylephrine is pure α-1 and useful as a push-dose agent for transient post-induction hypotension, but it can lower cardiac output in a weak heart. Dopamine causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine and is no longer first-line in septic shock.

For weight-based drips: mL/h = dose (mcg/kg/min) × weight (kg) × 60 ÷ concentration (mcg/mL). For example, norepinephrine 4 mg in 250 mL is 16 mcg/mL; 0.1 mcg/kg/min for 80 kg = 0.1 × 80 × 60 ÷ 16 = 30 mL/h.

Non-weight-based: mL/h = dose per hour ÷ concentration. Use smart pumps with drug libraries where available, double-check high-alert infusions with a second clinician, and label every line at the patient end. Before transport, change bags that will run out during the trip and calculate the volume needed plus a reserve.

Warfarin: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) plus IV vitamin K for life-threatening bleeding; plasma if PCC is unavailable. Heparin: protamine (about 1 mg per 100 units given in the last few hours; partial effect for low-molecular-weight heparin). Dabigatran: idarucizumab. Factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban): andexanet alfa where available, or PCC per protocol.

Thrombolytics (alteplase, tenecteplase) cause bleeding that may need cryoprecipitate and antifibrinolytics. Antiplatelet drugs are not reversed by PCC; platelet transfusion has a limited and selective role. In intracranial haemorrhage, reversal is time-critical.

Consolidate infusions onto transport pumps before leaving, and verify each against the order. Avoid stopping vasopressors during transfers — a brief interruption can drop pressure. Run critical drips through dedicated lines; do not bolus through a line carrying a vasopressor. Peripheral vasopressors in a good, proximal vein are acceptable short-term with site checks; extravasation of norepinephrine is treated with phentolamine infiltration per protocol.
Altitude can affect drip chambers and pressure bags; pumps eliminate most gravity-based errors. Battery life and oxygen supply should exceed the planned transport time with a margin.

Push-dose vasopressors bridge brief hypotension — post-induction, during sedation, or while an infusion is prepared. Phenylephrine is commonly prepared at 100 mcg/mL and given in 50–200 mcg boluses; dilute epinephrine is prepared at 10 mcg/mL (for example 1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL epinephrine added to 9 mL of saline) and given in 5–20 mcg boluses. Preparation errors are a recognised hazard: use standard recipes, label syringes clearly, and double-check.
Push-dose pressors are a bridge, not a treatment plan. If repeated boluses are needed, start an infusion and treat the cause — volume, haemorrhage, sepsis, or the induction agent.

Ventilated patients need analgesia first, then sedation titrated to a target such as a Richmond Agitation–Sedation Scale (RASS) of −1 to −2 for most, deeper (−4 to −5) when paralysed or for raised ICP. Common infusions: fentanyl 25–200 mcg/h, propofol 5–50 mcg/kg/min (watch blood pressure and triglycerides on prolonged use), midazolam 1–10 mg/h (accumulates in renal and hepatic failure), ketamine 0.5–2 mg/kg/h (haemodynamically supportive), and dexmedetomidine 0.2–1.5 mcg/kg/h (bradycardia and hypotension; little respiratory depression).

Paralysed patients must be deeply sedated; check that sedation infusions are running before any redose of a paralytic. In flight, stimuli are greater and patients may need more; reassess at regular intervals and before landing and transfer.

Two large-bore peripheral IVs serve most resuscitations; flow depends on catheter radius and length (Poiseuille), so a short 14–16 gauge peripheral line outflows a long, narrow central lumen. Intraosseous (IO) access is fast and reliable when veins fail — proximal humerus, proximal or distal tibia, and the sternum in some devices. Humeral IO gives higher flow and faster central delivery than tibial. Flush, give lidocaine for pain in awake patients per protocol, and use a pressure bag for flow.

Central venous catheters (internal jugular, subclavian, femoral) allow vasopressors, multiple infusions, CVP monitoring and central venous saturation. Ultrasound guidance reduces complications. Subclavian lines carry the highest pneumothorax risk; femoral lines the highest infection risk; the internal jugular sits in between and is accessible with ultrasound.

An arterial line gives beat-to-beat pressure and arterial sampling — valuable on vasopressors, in labile patients and where non-invasive cuffs fail in vibration. The radial artery is preferred; femoral and brachial are alternatives. Complications include thrombosis, distal ischaemia, infection, haematoma and accidental drug injection.

Level the transducer to the phlebostatic axis (4th intercostal space, mid-axillary line) and zero it to atmosphere. A transducer below the heart reads falsely high; above reads falsely low — roughly 7.4 mmHg per 10 cm. Re-level after every position change, and remember aircraft cabin pressure changes do not affect a properly zeroed system once rezeroed at altitude per protocol.

Perform a square-wave (fast-flush) test: one to two oscillations then return to the waveform indicates optimal damping. Many oscillations mean underdamping (systolic overestimated); a slow return with no oscillation means overdamping (bubble, clot, kink, soft pressure bag; systolic underestimated). The mean arterial pressure is least affected by damping.

CVP approximates right atrial pressure (normal about 2–8 mmHg). Read it at end-expiration. A high CVP occurs with RV failure, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, pulmonary hypertension, volume overload and high PEEP; a low CVP suggests hypovolaemia. CVP alone predicts fluid responsiveness poorly; trends and context matter.

Pulmonary artery catheters measure right-sided pressures, PA pressure (normal about 15–30 systolic / 4–12 diastolic), pulmonary artery occlusion ("wedge") pressure approximating left atrial pressure (about 6–12), cardiac output and mixed venous saturation (SvO₂ about 65–75 %). A wedge above about 18 with low cardiac index points to cardiogenic shock; low wedge with low output points to hypovolaemia; low SVR with high output points to distributive shock.

In transport, a PA catheter must never be left in the wedge position (balloon inflated) — it risks pulmonary infarction and rupture. Watch the waveform: a damped, wedged trace when the balloon is deflated means the catheter has migrated distally; pull it back per protocol. Secure catheters carefully; migration is common with movement.

Air embolism: air entering a central line (especially with the patient upright or during disconnection) causes sudden hypoxia, hypotension and arrest. Clamp the line, place the patient left lateral and head down (Durant's manoeuvre), give 100 % oxygen, and aspirate from the catheter if possible.

Dislodgement and bleeding: secure lines and tubing before moves; a dislodged arterial line can bleed briskly. Infection: maintain aseptic handling. Pneumothorax after a recent subclavian or IJ insertion may declare itself at altitude as trapped air expands.

Confirm the patient, date and projection (AP films magnify the heart and are standard in ICU and transport; PA films are standard in clinics). Check rotation (spinous processes centred between clavicle heads) and inspiration (about 9–10 posterior ribs visible).

Then a fixed sequence, so nothing is skipped: tubes and lines; airway (trachea midline?); breathing (lung fields, pleural spaces, costophrenic angles, apices for pneumothorax); cardiac silhouette and mediastinum; diaphragm (free air beneath?); everything else (bones, soft tissues, surgical emphysema).

Pneumothorax: a visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it; on a supine film, look for a deep sulcus sign (a deep, lucent costophrenic angle). Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, but a film may show mediastinal shift away and a flattened hemidiaphragm. Any pneumothorax will expand at altitude (Boyle's law); drain before flight per programme policy.

Haemothorax and effusion: blunting of the costophrenic angle on an upright film; on a supine film, a diffuse haziness of one hemithorax. Pulmonary oedema: bilateral perihilar ("bat-wing") opacities, cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines and upper-lobe diversion in cardiogenic oedema; ARDS tends to be more peripheral with a normal heart size. Consolidation: a lobar opacity with air bronchograms.

Widened mediastinum (above about 8 cm on a PA film, though AP films magnify) with blunt deceleration raises concern for aortic injury. Free air under the diaphragm on an upright film indicates a perforated viscus. Gastric distension on a film before flight warrants a gastric tube.

On CT, density is measured in Hounsfield units: air is about −1000, fat about −100, water 0, acute blood about 40–80 (bright on non-contrast CT), bone +1000. Fresh intracranial blood is bright; acute ischaemic stroke may look normal early. An epidural haematoma is biconvex (lens-shaped) and does not cross sutures; a subdural is crescentic and crosses sutures but not the midline falx.

Ask the referring team for the formal report and send images with the patient. Your job is to recognise findings that change care en route — expanding blood, pneumothorax, free air, tube position — not to provide a formal read.
An intubated pneumonia patient's pre-transfer film shows: ETT tip 1 cm above the carina, a 15 % right apical pneumothorax after a recent IJ line, and a gastric tube coiled in the oesophagus.

Two patients are ready for transfer. Patient A, after a fall: supine film with a deep, lucent left costophrenic angle and subcutaneous emphysema. Patient B, with sepsis: bilateral peripheral opacities, normal heart size, ETT tip at the level of the clavicles, central line tip in the right atrium deep.

Bedside ultrasound images increasingly travel with the patient. Recognise the key findings: a pericardial effusion as a black stripe around the heart (with right ventricular diastolic collapse in tamponade); free fluid in Morison's pouch on a FAST; absent lung sliding and a barcode M-mode in pneumothorax; B-lines in interstitial oedema; and an abdominal aorta wider than 3 cm.
Ultrasound is operator-dependent; record who performed it and when, and repeat if the patient changes. A negative FAST does not rule out haemorrhage, particularly retroperitoneal.

Glycolysis in the cytoplasm turns glucose into pyruvate and a small amount of ATP (two per glucose) without oxygen. With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondria, feeds the Krebs (citric acid) cycle, and the electron transport chain uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor to produce most of the cell's ATP (roughly 30–36 per glucose) and CO₂ and water.

Without enough oxygen — or when mitochondria are poisoned (cyanide) — pyruvate is converted to lactate to keep glycolysis running. Lactate rises; ATP falls. This is why hypoperfusion causes lactic acidosis, and why restoring oxygen delivery, not just blood pressure, is the goal of resuscitation.

Haemoglobin binding is cooperative, giving a sigmoid curve. On the flat upper part, a large fall in PaO₂ barely changes saturation (90 % saturation at about 60 mmHg). On the steep part, small falls in PaO₂ release large amounts of oxygen — good for tissues, but meaning saturation can fall quickly once PaO₂ drops below about 60.

A right shift (lower affinity, more oxygen released to tissues) occurs with acidosis, raised CO₂, fever and increased 2,3-DPG — the Bohr effect helps active tissues. A left shift (higher affinity, less release) occurs with alkalosis, low CO₂, hypothermia, low 2,3-DPG (stored blood), carbon monoxide and fetal haemoglobin.

Oxygen content is mostly bound to haemoglobin: CaO₂ ≈ (1.34 × Hb × SaO₂) + (0.003 × PaO₂). Delivery is content × cardiac output. Raising PaO₂ above full saturation adds little oxygen, except in hyperbaric therapy.

Ideal gas exchange matches ventilation (V) to perfusion (Q). Low V/Q units (pneumonia, atelectasis) and shunt (V/Q = 0: flooded or collapsed alveoli, intracardiac shunt) cause hypoxaemia. V/Q mismatch improves with oxygen; true shunt barely does and needs recruitment.

Dead space (V/Q = ∞: pulmonary embolism, low cardiac output, overdistension) wastes ventilation and raises the PaCO₂–EtCO₂ gap. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated regions; vasodilators can worsen V/Q matching by abolishing it.
The alveolar gas equation (PAO₂ = FiO₂ × (Pb − 47) − PaCO₂/0.8) explains why altitude (lower barometric pressure, Pb) and hypoventilation (higher PaCO₂) lower alveolar oxygen even with normal lungs.

Spontaneous inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, drawing venous blood into the chest and augmenting right-heart filling. Positive-pressure ventilation does the opposite: it raises intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and right-ventricular preload while lowering left-ventricular afterload. Hypovolaemic patients therefore become hypotensive after intubation, while patients with LV failure may improve on positive pressure.

High PEEP, auto-PEEP and tension pneumothorax all raise intrathoracic pressure and can cause obstructive shock. In tamponade, spontaneous inspiration fills the RV, shifts the septum and reduces LV output — pulsus paradoxus. Pulse-pressure variation on controlled ventilation reflects preload responsiveness.

CO₂ travels in three forms: about 70 % as bicarbonate (formed in red cells by carbonic anhydrase), about 20–23 % bound to haemoglobin as carbamino compounds, and 7–10 % dissolved. Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO₂ (the Haldane effect), which helps load CO₂ in the tissues and unload it in the lungs.

Giving high-flow oxygen to some patients with chronic CO₂ retention can raise PaCO₂ through the Haldane effect, worsened V/Q matching (loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) and, to a lesser degree, reduced drive. Target SpO₂ 88–92 % in known retainers while treating the cause.

Ventilation controls PaCO₂ within minutes: halving alveolar ventilation roughly doubles PaCO₂. That is why EtCO₂ responds quickly to rate changes on the ventilator, while bicarbonate adjustment by the kidneys takes days.

Read every ECG the same way so nothing is missed. Rate: 300 divided by the number of large boxes between R waves, or count complexes in 10 seconds and multiply by six. Rhythm: regular or irregular, P before every QRS, QRS after every P. Axis: normal if leads I and aVF are both positive; left axis deviation if I is positive and aVF negative (with lead II negative); right axis deviation if I is negative and aVF positive.

Intervals: PR 120–200 ms; QRS under 120 ms; QTc under about 450 ms in men and 460–470 in women (above 500 is high risk for torsades). Then morphology: P waves, Q waves, QRS width and pattern (bundle branch blocks), R-wave progression, and finally the ST segments and T waves.

STEMI criteria (in the absence of LVH or LBBB): new ST elevation at the J point in two contiguous leads of at least 1 mm, except in V2–V3 where the thresholds are 2 mm in men 40 or older, 2.5 mm in men under 40, and 1.5 mm in women. Reciprocal ST depression in the opposite territory increases specificity.

Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) is usually the right coronary artery (or circumflex in left-dominant systems); obtain right-sided leads (V4R) to look for right-ventricular infarction, which makes the patient preload-dependent — avoid nitrates and give fluid for hypotension. ST elevation in III greater than II and reciprocal depression in I and aVL favour the RCA. Anterior STEMI (V1–V4) is the LAD; lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6) the circumflex or diagonal. Posterior infarction shows ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3; confirm with posterior leads V7–V9 (ST elevation ≥ 0.5 mm).

Some occlusions do not meet classic criteria. Widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR suggests left main or multivessel ischaemia. De Winter T waves — upsloping ST depression with tall, symmetric T waves in the precordial leads — indicate proximal LAD occlusion. Wellens pattern (deep symmetric or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 in a pain-free patient) warns of critical proximal LAD stenosis.
