Translational lift: above about 16–24 knots of airspeed, the rotor moves into undisturbed air and becomes markedly more efficient — the aircraft shudders briefly and then climbs more easily. Ground effect: within about one rotor diameter of a firm, level surface, downwash is cushioned and less power is needed to hover. Hovering out of ground effect (over long grass, water, or high above a scene) requires far more power.

Settling with power (vortex ring state) occurs when a helicopter descends vertically or near-vertically at low airspeed while using power: it settles into its own downwash, and adding power makes the descent worse. Recovery requires forward airspeed. Approaches to confined landing zones are planned to avoid steep, slow descents — one reason a pilot may refuse a tight landing site.

Dynamic rollover occurs when a skid or wheel is pinned on the ground (on a slope, in mud or by a tie-down) and the aircraft pivots around it, rolling over beyond recovery within seconds. Landing zones should be firm and level, and crew must never hold or lean on the aircraft during lift-off.

Autorotation is the controlled descent of a helicopter after engine failure: the pilot lowers the collective, and upward airflow through the rotor keeps it turning, like a sycamore seed. Just before touchdown the pilot raises the nose and collective to use the rotor's stored energy to cushion the landing. A successful autorotation requires height and airspeed; the "height–velocity diagram" (the "dead man's curve") defines low-and-slow combinations from which a safe autorotation is impossible. Crew should be seated and restrained with helmets on during take-off and landing, the phases of greatest risk.
Ground crews have set up a landing zone in a small clearing surrounded by 25-metre trees, on a slight slope, on a hot afternoon. The pilot circles twice, then elects to land at a field 1 km away.

Airplanes generate lift with fixed wings and need forward speed to fly; take-off and landing distances depend on weight, density altitude, runway surface and wind. Flaps increase lift and drag at low speeds for take-off and landing. The airplane stalls if its angle of attack exceeds the critical angle, regardless of speed — most likely at low speed during approach and departure.

Turbulence and wind shear near the ground can cause sudden loss of airspeed and altitude. Crew should be seated with belts fastened during take-off, landing and turbulence; unsecured equipment becomes a projectile in severe turbulence, and in-flight injuries to crew are most often from turbulence while standing.

Pressurisation allows high-altitude cruise above most weather; the cabin altitude is maintained by a pressure differential that the airframe is designed to hold. The pilot can fly lower or set a lower cabin altitude for patients who need it, at the cost of fuel and speed.

Density altitude is the altitude at which the aircraft "feels" it is flying, given the actual air density. It rises with elevation, temperature and humidity. A helipad at 5000 feet on a 35 °C day may have a density altitude above 8000 feet. Thinner air means the rotor produces less lift, the engine produces less power, and the aircraft needs more power to hover, climb and land.

"High, hot and humid" days reduce payload, climb rate and hover capability, and may make hovering out of ground effect impossible. The pilot calculates performance from charts for the conditions and may need to reduce weight — leaving a crew member, equipment or fuel behind — or decline the flight.

Pressure altitude (altimeter set to 29.92 inHg or 1013 hPa) corrected for non-standard temperature gives density altitude. Standard temperature at sea level is 15 °C and falls about 2 °C per 1000 feet; every degree above standard raises density altitude by roughly 120 feet.

Every aircraft has a maximum gross weight (for take-off and landing) and a centre of gravity (CG) envelope. Exceeding weight reduces performance and structural margins; a CG outside limits can make the aircraft uncontrollable, especially in helicopters, where cyclic authority to correct an out-of-limit CG is limited.

The medical crew influence both: crew weights, the patient's weight (including obese patients and those with heavy equipment such as balloon pumps, ECMO or incubators), family members, additional providers, blood coolers and bags. Report accurate weights before the flight and before adding anything. Secure equipment where the configuration places it; moving heavy items changes the CG.
Fuel is part of the weight calculation. On a hot day at a high helipad, the pilot may carry less fuel to stay within limits, which shortens range and requires a refuelling plan.

Fuel planning includes the trip, contingencies, a reserve and, in instrument conditions, fuel to fly to an alternate airport. Under FAA rules, helicopters operating under visual flight rules need enough fuel to reach the first intended landing plus at least 20 minutes at normal cruise (Part 135), and many air medical operators require 30 minutes or more; instrument flights require fuel to the destination, then to an alternate, plus 30 minutes. Many air medical operators set stricter reserves.

Fuel consumption rises with weight, wind, hovering and high power settings. A long scene hover, a diversion or a headwind can shorten range unexpectedly. The medical crew can help by being ready when the aircraft lands (minimising ground running time) and by understanding that a "minimum fuel" call means the plan must change — not that the pilot is being cautious for no reason.

A 190 kg patient needs transfer from a hospital helipad at 6500 feet on a 30 °C afternoon. The referring team also wants a respiratory therapist to accompany, with a transport ventilator and two infusion pumps.

Pilots use performance charts to find the maximum weight at which the aircraft can hover in ground effect (HIGE) and out of ground effect (HOGE) for the expected temperature and pressure altitude at each landing site. Confined or elevated LZs, or those surrounded by obstacles, may require HOGE performance, which is significantly more demanding.

Power margin is the difference between the power available and the power required. Large margins allow for gusts, go-arounds and unexpected obstacles. Small margins leave no room for error. Air medical programmes often specify minimum margins and may restrict operations on hot afternoons or at high-altitude hospitals.

As fuel burns off, weight falls and performance improves, so return flights may be easier than outbound ones. Conversely, adding a patient, extra crew and equipment at a hot scene at the end of a long flight can be the most demanding moment of the mission. Plan the whole mission, not just the first leg.

Fire is one of the most feared in-flight emergencies because the aircraft cannot simply stop. Sources include electrical faults, oxygen-enriched environments, medical equipment and engine fires. Tell the pilot immediately and precisely ("smoke from the ventilator", "burning smell behind the left seat"), turn off oxygen if it is feeding the fire, and isolate electrical power to the suspected equipment if you can.

Use the aircraft fire extinguisher (typically Halon or a Halon replacement) aimed at the base of the fire. In a small cabin, extinguishing agents and smoke displace oxygen and can be toxic: crew may need to use portable oxygen or protective breathing equipment, and the pilot may open vents to clear smoke. Most air medical aircraft will land as soon as possible after any fire or smoke event.
Engine fires are managed by the pilot from the cockpit with fire handles and bottles; the crew's role is to prepare for an emergency landing and evacuation.

Rapid (explosive) decompression follows a sudden loss of cabin pressure — a failed window or door seal. Signs: a loud bang, a rush of air, fog in the cabin (water vapour condensing as temperature falls), flying debris and cold. Cabin altitude climbs toward aircraft altitude within seconds, and the time of useful consciousness at 25 000 feet is only 3–5 minutes (much less with activity). Slow decompression is insidious: a gradually rising cabin altitude, ear pressure and hypoxia symptoms in crew, detected by the cabin altitude warning.

Response: crew put on their own oxygen masks first — you cannot help a patient if you are hypoxic — then secure the patient's oxygen (increase FiO₂ to 100 %), check ventilator function, and stay seated and restrained. The pilot performs an emergency descent to a safe altitude (usually 10 000 feet or lower). Afterwards, reassess the patient for gas expansion effects: pneumothorax, ETT cuff over-inflation, and air in infusion lines and drains.

Inadvertent instrument meteorological conditions (IIMC) — flying unintentionally into cloud or fog, losing outside visual reference — has historically been a leading cause of fatal helicopter air ambulance accidents through spatial disorientation and controlled flight into terrain. The pilot's recovery procedure is to transition immediately to instruments, level the aircraft, climb to a safe altitude, turn away if appropriate and contact air traffic control. Crew support this with sterile cabin, readiness to read out instruments if asked, and an "IIMC" call when they see visual references disappearing. Prevention — conservative weather minimums and willingness to turn back early — is far more effective than recovery.

Emergency landing: the pilot announces the emergency and an expected time to landing. Crew secure loose equipment, stop non-essential care, tighten restraints, put on helmets with visors down, and adopt the brace position appropriate to the seat (typically feet flat, back against the seat, head against the headrest or bent forward depending on seat design and orientation). Secure the patient's restraints and cover their face if possible.

After landing: wait until the aircraft has stopped moving and the rotors have stopped, unless there is fire. Disconnect the patient from aircraft systems, exit by the nearest safe exit (know the emergency exits and how to open them), move upwind and away from the aircraft, and account for everyone. Activate the emergency locator transmitter if it has not triggered automatically, and begin survival procedures.

Twenty minutes into a fixed-wing flight at FL250 (cabin altitude 7000 ft), the crew notices a burning smell, then light smoke from behind the infusion pump mount. The patient is ventilated on 60 % oxygen.

Bird strikes can crack windscreens, damage rotors and disable crew; visors down reduce eye injury. A door opening in flight — usually from an incompletely latched door — can cause loss of equipment, injury and control problems; do not try to close it in flight unless the pilot directs it, and keep away from the opening.

Medical emergencies affecting the pilot (incapacitation) are rare but possible; crew should know how to communicate with ATC and the company, and some programmes train medical crew in basic aircraft control and radio use for this reason. Smoke or fumes from the patient's equipment, oxygen leaks and lithium battery fires (thermal runaway in devices) are increasingly recognised; batteries that swell, smoke or overheat should be isolated, and the pilot informed.

Laser strikes from the ground can dazzle the pilot and cause eye injury. Report immediately; avoid looking toward the source, and the pilot may hand over or climb away. Such events are reported to ATC and law enforcement.

A typical recommended landing zone is at least 100 × 100 feet (about 30 × 30 metres) by day, often larger at night or for larger aircraft — operators set their own minimums. The surface should be firm, level (slope less than about 8–10°) and free of loose debris that the rotor wash will lift — blankets, sheets, plastic, gravel, snow and dust. Approach and departure paths should be clear of wires, towers, trees and poles; wires are the hardest hazard to see from the air.

Mark the corners with weighted cones or lights, and for night landings use lights that do not dazzle — never shine lights or spotlights at the aircraft. Do not use flares where there is fire risk. Keep vehicles and bystanders at least 100–200 feet away, with emergency vehicles positioned to protect the site but outside the rotor arc. Wet the ground in dusty conditions if possible.

Ground crews should brief the aircraft by radio with: the LZ location (GPS coordinates or a landmark), size and surface, obstacles (wires, poles, trees, towers), wind direction and strength, the slope, other aircraft or drones, and any hazards such as hazardous materials or crowds.

Approach a running helicopter only when signalled by the pilot or crew, and only from the front or side within the pilot's view — the "safe zone" is typically from the 10 o'clock to the 2 o'clock position, or as specified by the aircraft type. Never approach from the rear: the tail rotor is invisible when turning and lethal. On sloping ground, approach and leave on the downhill side, because the main rotor is closer to the ground on the uphill side.

Wear helmet and eye protection, secure loose clothing and items, carry long objects (IV poles, splints) horizontally below waist height, and never raise anything above your head. Do not run. Hold onto stretcher linen and loose equipment. No smoking within 50–100 feet of the aircraft.

Hot loading (with rotors turning) shortens scene times but increases risk; many programmes restrict it to trained crews and critical patients. Cold loading (engines shut down) is safer and used when the patient is not time critical or the ground crew is unfamiliar with the aircraft.

Night operations reduce depth perception and make wires invisible; NVG-equipped crews still depend on accurate ground briefings. Whiteout (snow) and brownout (dust) occur when rotor wash lifts loose surface material and obscures the ground during landing — a major cause of landing accidents and dynamic rollover. Wet or freeze the surface, or choose a paved area.

Hazardous materials scenes need upwind, uphill LZs well away from the release; the aircraft must not land in a contaminated area or blow contaminants around. At crash or fire scenes, smoke reduces visibility and can contain toxins. Crowds and media should be held well back. Drones near a scene are a serious collision risk — the aircraft should be told about any in the area.

Hospital helipads have their own procedures: rooftop pads have fire suppression, specific approach paths and often require a security escort. Crews should know the elevator access and how to leave the pad quickly in an emergency.

Fire crews have closed a motorway and propose an LZ on the carriageway near an overpass, with power lines crossing 200 metres to the east. Wind is from the west. There is loose debris from a crash and two drones overhead from bystanders.

Hospital helipads are designed for specific aircraft sizes and weights; rooftop pads have structural limits, fuel spill containment, fire suppression and defined approach and departure paths. Staff working on the pad must be trained in helicopter safety and fire response. Many hospitals require security to control access during landings.

Unfamiliar sites — first-time scenes, hospitals without a helipad, sports fields, car parks — carry more risk. A high and slow reconnaissance pass identifies wires, slopes, debris and people before committing to land. The pilot may ask the medical crew to watch specific obstacles during the approach.

After landing at a scene, the crew agree where the aircraft will stay (engines running or shut down), who stays with it, and how the patient will be brought to it. Bystanders and responders should not approach without an escort. Before departure, a final walk-around of the LZ checks for debris and people.

Air medical helicopters spend much of their time below 1000 feet, often at night, near scenes and hospitals surrounded by wires, towers, cranes, trees and buildings. Wire strikes are a leading cause of helicopter accidents: wires are thin, often unmarked, span valleys and roads, and blend into the background. Towers are usually lit and charted; the guy wires that support them are not.

Controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) — an airworthy aircraft flown into the ground, water or an obstacle without the crew realising — occurs most often at night, in poor visibility and in unfamiliar terrain. Mid-air collisions occur near hospitals, airports and scenes where several aircraft (other air ambulances, police, news helicopters and drones) converge.

Clues to wires: poles or pylons on either side of a road or river, cleared strips through trees, and buildings that must have power. Assume wires exist between any two poles, and around any farm, building or road.

Helicopter terrain awareness and warning systems (HTAWS), required for US helicopter air ambulances since the 2014 FAA rule, compare the aircraft's position and altitude with a terrain and obstacle database and give aural and visual alerts. Traffic collision avoidance or traffic advisory systems (TCAS/TAS) and ADS-B show nearby transponder-equipped aircraft. Radar altimeters give height above the ground. Wire-strike protection systems (cutters above and below the cockpit) can cut some wires on impact.

Databases are incomplete — new cranes, temporary towers and most wires are not included — and drones are usually invisible to traffic systems. Technology supplements but does not replace a disciplined visual scan, especially during low-level manoeuvring and landing.
Night vision goggles extend vision at night but have a limited field of view and poor contrast for thin wires; they are discussed in their own lesson.

The human eye detects movement and objects best when it stops: use a systematic scan of 10–15° sectors, pausing about one second in each, across the field of view. An aircraft on a collision course appears stationary in the windscreen while growing larger — "constant bearing, decreasing range" — which makes it hard to notice.

Use clock positions relative to the aircraft's nose (12 o'clock straight ahead, 3 o'clock right, 9 o'clock left), with a high/low/level indication and range: "Traffic, 2 o'clock, high, two miles, converging." "Wires, 12 o'clock low, crossing the road ahead." Speak calmly, clearly and early; the pilot will acknowledge. If you see an immediate threat, the call should be direct: "Climb!", "Stop!", or as agreed by your programme.

Medical crew are expected to stop patient care to look out during take-off, approach and landing, and when the pilot asks for help — patient care is paused for the minute it takes to land safely. Clear your side of the aircraft verbally at the LZ: "Clear left, tail clear."

At night, the helicopter is descending toward a scene LZ in a river valley. You notice two pylons on the valley sides ahead and to the right, with no visible wires between them. The HTAWS shows no obstacle alert.

At night, the eye relies on rods in the peripheral retina, which detect light and motion but not detail or colour; a dark wire or unlit tower against dark terrain may be completely invisible. Lights on obstacles help, but failed lights are common and unlit structures exist. NVGs extend vision but do not reliably show wires.

Black-hole approaches — over water or unlit terrain toward a lit LZ — create the illusion of being higher than you are, leading to low approaches into obstacles or terrain. Featureless terrain, snow and water make height judgement difficult. Pilots rely on instruments, radar altimeters and stabilised approach criteria.

Medical crew contribute by keeping the cabin dark, scanning their side during approach and departure, and calling out anything that might be an obstacle — it is better to report a false alarm than miss a real hazard. Familiarity with regularly used LZs and hospitals, including new construction, is shared through briefings and the SMS.

A common framework is the "rule of threes": a person can survive about 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in harsh conditions, 3 days without water and 3 weeks without food. The order of priorities follows: first aid and safety, shelter, signalling, water, then food. Most survivors of air medical accidents are found within 24–72 hours, so the aim is to stay alive, stay together and be found.

Immediately after a crash or forced landing: get everyone out and away from the aircraft if there is fire or fuel risk, account for all crew and the patient, give first aid, and then decide whether to return to the aircraft. Once fire risk has passed, the aircraft is your best shelter, signal and supply cache — it is far easier to see from the air than people.

Stay with the aircraft unless it is unsafe or you are certain of rescue nearby. Moving away makes you harder to find and exposes the group to injury and exhaustion. A positive mental attitude, leadership and keeping busy improve survival as much as equipment.

Hypothermia kills faster than thirst or hunger in most environments. Get out of wind and wet, insulate from the ground (heat is lost fastest by conduction to cold ground), wear all available layers, use survival blankets, and huddle together. In hot climates, shelter from the sun, minimise exertion during the day and conserve sweat.

The emergency locator transmitter (ELT) activates on impact (or manually) and transmits on 406 MHz to satellites, which locate it within a few kilometres; flight-following systems will also show the last known position. Other signals: radios, mobile and satellite phones, signal mirrors (visible for many miles in sunlight), flares and smoke, fires in a triangle (an international distress signal), bright panels and large ground symbols — "V" means assistance needed, "X" means medical assistance needed.

Water: ration sweat, not water — drink what you need. Collect rain and dew; boil or purify surface water where possible. Fire provides warmth, signalling, water purification and morale; build it in a sheltered spot away from the aircraft and fuel. Food is low priority in the short term.

Helicopters are top-heavy and often roll inverted soon after ditching. Before impact: helmets on, restraints tight, brace, and locate your exit with a hand on a reference point (the exit or the frame near it). After impact, wait for violent motion to stop, then release your restraint, open the exit and swim out, keeping hold of a reference point. Underwater egress training and emergency breathing devices (small compressed air cylinders) significantly improve survival.

Do not inflate a life vest inside the aircraft — it will pin you against the ceiling of an inverted cabin. Inflate it once outside. Stay together in the water, link arms, and use the HELP (heat escape lessening posture) or huddle to reduce heat loss. Cold water shock — gasping and hyperventilation in the first minute — is a major cause of drowning; control breathing before swimming.
Life rafts may be carried on aircraft flying over water; deploy and board them, keep the group together, and activate signalling devices.

Your helicopter makes a precautionary landing in a snowy valley after a chip light (metal particles in the gearbox oil). Everyone is uninjured; the patient is a stable orthopaedic transfer. Temperature −8 °C, wind 20 knots, two hours of daylight left. Phones have no signal.

Aircraft survival kits are tailored to the operating area: shelter (emergency blankets, bivvy bags), signalling (mirror, whistle, strobe, flares), fire-starting materials, water and purification, food bars, a knife or multi-tool, a first aid kit, cordage and, over water, flotation and rafts. Know where the kit is and what is in it; carry a small personal kit on your flight suit in case you cannot reach the aircraft.

Cold environments: prevent sweating (remove layers when working), keep dry, insulate from the ground, and watch for hypothermia and frostbite in the group. Hot environments: shade, minimal exertion during the heat of the day, and conserve water in the body by limiting sweating rather than rationing drinking. Desert nights can be very cold.
Psychological factors matter. Fear, pain, fatigue and boredom degrade decision-making. Clear leadership, assigning tasks, keeping the group together and maintaining hope are important survival tools.

Ceiling is the height above the ground of the lowest layer of cloud reported as broken (5–7 eighths of the sky covered) or overcast (8 eighths). Visibility is the horizontal distance you can see. Visual flight rules (VFR) require the pilot to see and avoid terrain, obstacles and other aircraft; instrument flight rules (IFR) allow flight in cloud by reference to instruments with air traffic control separation, but require an IFR-equipped aircraft, an instrument-rated pilot and suitable approaches at the destination.

US helicopter air ambulance weather minimums under Part 135 are stricter than for other operations and vary by local or non-local area, mountainous or non-mountainous terrain, day or night, and use of night vision goggles or HTAWS — the table in 14 CFR 135.609 sets ceilings from several hundred feet up to 1500 feet and visibilities of several miles, with the highest minimums for unfamiliar mountainous areas at night. Many programmes add their own higher minimums.

Weather at the departure, en route, scene and destination all matter, as does the forecast for the return. A flight should not start if conditions are expected to fall below minimums during the mission.

Fog forms when air cools to its dew point near the ground. Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights and burns off after sunrise; advection fog forms when moist air moves over a cold surface (coastal areas) and can persist. A small temperature–dew point spread (within about 2–3 °C) warns that fog or low cloud is likely. Fog and low cloud are major factors in IIMC accidents.

Icing: supercooled water droplets freeze on contact with the airframe and rotor blades, adding weight, destroying lift and blocking intakes. Most air medical helicopters are not certified for flight into known icing, so visible moisture at temperatures near or below freezing is a no-go. Thunderstorms produce severe turbulence, lightning, hail, wind shear, microbursts and heavy rain; aircraft should stay at least 20 miles from severe storms.

Wind affects groundspeed, fuel, landing direction and turbulence. Mechanical turbulence occurs downwind of buildings, trees and ridges; mountain wave turbulence on the lee side of mountains can be severe. Gusty winds make hovering and landing in confined areas hazardous. Whiteout (snow) and brownout (dust) reduce visibility at landing.

A METAR is a routine surface observation, usually hourly; a SPECI is a special observation when conditions change significantly. A TAF is an airport forecast covering 24–30 hours, using change groups (FM — from, TEMPO — temporary, PROB — probability). Other tools include graphical forecasts, the HEMS weather tool (which shows ceilings and visibility between reporting stations), radar, satellite, and pilot reports (PIREPs) — the only direct observation of conditions aloft.

Reporting stations can be far apart, and conditions between them — especially in valleys, near water and over high ground — may be worse than reported. Crews should report deteriorating weather on the way to a scene and support a decision to turn back. A weather turn-down is a sound decision, not a failure: the "weather decline" should be communicated to the requesting agency and any subsequent service.
A request comes at 04:00. The destination METAR reads: 180350Z 00000KT 4SM BR SCT004 BKN009 08/07 A3012. The TAF includes "TEMPO 0507 1/2SM FG OVC002".

Weather patterns vary with season and geography. Winter brings icing, snow, freezing fog and short daylight; summer brings convective thunderstorms in the afternoon and evening, high density altitude and haze; spring and autumn bring frontal systems and rapidly changing conditions. Coastal areas have advection fog and sea breezes; mountainous areas have mountain waves, valley fog, rapidly changing local weather and lower effective minimums.

Fronts: a cold front often brings a narrow band of thunderstorms, gusty winds and a sharp improvement afterwards; a warm front brings widespread low cloud, drizzle and poor visibility over a broad area ahead of it. Low-pressure systems are associated with cloud and precipitation; high pressure with clearer skies but also radiation fog and haze.
Local knowledge — which valleys fill with fog at dawn, which hospitals are often in low cloud — is valuable. Share it in briefings and through programme weather resources.

Turbine helicopters and turboprops burn jet fuel (Jet A, a kerosene-based fuel); piston aircraft burn aviation gasoline (avgas). Putting the wrong fuel in an aircraft can cause engine failure — the fuel type is checked at every fill, and nozzles are designed to make misfuelling harder. Jet fuel has a higher flash point than gasoline but its vapour is still flammable, especially in hot conditions.

Static electricity builds up as fuel flows through hoses and filters. Bonding — connecting the fuel truck or nozzle and the aircraft with a cable before opening the fuel cap — equalises their electrical potential so that a spark does not jump at the filler. Grounding is not a substitute for bonding. Do not use mobile phones, radios or other potential ignition sources near the refuelling point, and no smoking within at least 50 feet.

A fire extinguisher must be available and staffed during refuelling. Know the location of the fuel shut-off and how to stop the flow in an emergency. Fuel spills are reported and cleaned up according to local procedure; do not start engines in a spill area.

Hot refuelling — refuelling with engines running and rotors turning — saves time on long missions but adds risk: rotor hazards, noise, and a running engine as an ignition source. It is done only by trained personnel following the operator's procedures, with the pilot at the controls, a fire guard posted and communication between the fueller and pilot.

Patients should not normally be on board during refuelling. Where it is allowed by the operator (for example, critically ill patients who cannot be safely unloaded), it typically requires cold refuelling or specific approval, a medical crew member with the patient, all doors on the refuelling side closed and the opposite side door open or ready for evacuation, oxygen secured, and no electrical equipment connected or disconnected near the fuel point. Know your programme's policy before the situation arises.
Medical crew do not refuel unless trained and authorised. Their role is to keep the patient safe, stay clear of the fuelling area, watch for hazards and be ready to evacuate the patient.

Water in fuel — from condensation in tanks or contaminated supplies — can freeze, block filters or cause engine flame-out. Microbial growth in jet fuel produces sludge that blocks filters. Particulates damage fuel controls. Pilots or fuellers sample fuel from sumps before flight and after refuelling, checking for water (which settles at the bottom), sediment and the correct colour and smell.

Fuel from unfamiliar sources (for example, a remote airport or hospital fuel farm) should be checked for quality and the supplier's quality control. Additives such as fuel system icing inhibitor prevent water in jet fuel from freezing at altitude.

During a long interfacility transfer, the pilot needs to refuel at a regional airport. The ventilated patient is on oxygen and three infusions. The fueller is new and plans to start fuelling with the rotors turning while you remain on board with the patient.

A small spill should stop the refuelling and be contained with absorbent material before the engine is started. Larger spills require the area to be cleared, ignition sources removed and the airport or fire service notified. Fuel on clothing or skin is a fire and chemical hazard; remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin.

If a fire starts during refuelling: stop the fuel flow (emergency shut-off), raise the alarm, evacuate the patient and crew upwind, and use the extinguisher only if it is safe to do so and the fire is small. Do not move the aircraft unless instructed.

Fuel trucks and fixed fuel stations have emergency stop buttons; crew should know their location at regularly used sites. Refuelling during thunderstorms in the vicinity is suspended because of lightning risk.

Fatigue degrades reaction time, attention, memory, decision-making and communication — the skills that matter most at 03:00 on a hard mission. Being awake for 17–19 hours impairs performance about as much as a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05 %, and 24 hours awake is comparable to 0.1 %. Fatigued people are poor judges of their own impairment.

The circadian low occurs between roughly 02:00 and 06:00, when alertness is lowest regardless of how much sleep you had; a smaller dip occurs mid-afternoon. Night shifts, 24-hour shifts and rotating schedules disrupt sleep and accumulate sleep debt, which only sleep repays. Microsleeps — brief lapses of a few seconds — can occur without awareness.

Long-term shift work is associated with cardiovascular disease, metabolic disorders, mood disturbances and accidents on the drive home. Air medical programmes manage fatigue through scheduling, rest facilities, limits on duty time and policies that allow crew to decline flights when fatigued.

Pilots and crew use the IMSAFE checklist before each shift and flight: Illness (any symptoms, including colds that block the ears and sinuses — barotrauma risk at altitude), Medication (prescription and over-the-counter drugs that cause drowsiness, such as antihistamines), Stress (personal, financial, work), Alcohol (FAA pilots: no alcohol within 8 hours of flight — "8 hours bottle to throttle" — and a blood alcohol concentration below 0.04 %; many programmes extend this to 12 hours and apply it to all crew), Fatigue, and Emotion (or Eating — dehydration and hypoglycaemia also impair performance).

Recent scuba diving is a specific risk: flying soon after diving can cause decompression sickness. Common guidance is to wait at least 12 hours after a single no-decompression dive and 18 hours after multiple dives or multiple days of diving, longer after dives requiring decompression stops. Recent blood donation can reduce tolerance to hypoxia.

Physical fitness matters: crew lift stretchers and patients in awkward positions, often at night and in poor weather, and must be able to egress the aircraft in an emergency. Many programmes set weight limits (for aircraft performance and seat certification) and fitness standards.

Prioritise sleep: protect a 7–9 hour sleep opportunity before shifts, use dark, quiet, cool rooms, and keep a consistent routine on days off where possible. Strategic naps of 20–30 minutes improve alertness without deep-sleep grogginess; a longer nap of about 90 minutes covers a full sleep cycle. Caffeine helps when timed before the expected low and avoided within several hours of planned sleep. Bright light helps alertness during night shifts; dark glasses on the drive home help sleep afterwards.

Hydrate and eat regularly — small, balanced meals rather than heavy meals on night shifts. Team strategies include cross-checking each other, verbalising plans, and using checklists during the circadian low.

Standing down because of fatigue or illness is a professional decision. A just culture supports crew who remove themselves from duty without penalty; programmes should have backup procedures so that the service is not compromised. If you are too tired to drive home after a shift, use the rest facility or arrange transport.

It is 04:30 on the last night of three consecutive 24-hour shifts. You have slept for 2 hours in the past 22. A request comes in for an interfacility transfer. Your pilot says he feels fine. You notice you just read the same paragraph of the patient report three times.

Air medical crews are exposed repeatedly to trauma, death, child injury, and the stress of high-stakes decisions in difficult environments. Sleep disruption and fatigue amplify the effects. Burnout, depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress and substance misuse occur at higher rates in emergency services than in the general population.

Protective factors include peer support programmes, critical incident stress management, access to confidential counselling and employee assistance programmes, healthy sleep, exercise and social connection, and a culture where talking about stress is normal. Leaders who model asking for help reduce stigma.

Recognise warning signs in yourself and colleagues: withdrawal, irritability, changes in sleep or alcohol use, and loss of interest. Asking a colleague directly how they are doing is the first step. This topic is covered in depth in the professional domain's lesson on caregiver PTSD and suicide risk.

A safety management system (SMS) is a structured, organisation-wide approach to managing risk. Its four pillars are safety policy (leadership commitment and accountability), safety risk management (identifying hazards and controlling risk), safety assurance (monitoring, auditing and measuring performance) and safety promotion (training and communication). The FAA requires SMS for some operators and encourages it across air medical services; accreditation bodies expect it.

Heinrich's pyramid illustrates the idea that for every serious accident there are many minor incidents and hundreds of near-misses and unsafe acts. Accidents are usually the end of a chain of hazards and errors (Reason's "Swiss cheese" model): defences have holes, and an accident happens when the holes line up. Reporting near-misses allows the holes to be found and closed before they align.

A hazard is a condition that could cause harm (an unmarked wire near a regular LZ, a faulty stretcher lock); risk is the combination of the likelihood and severity of harm from that hazard. Risk matrices help prioritise action.

People report only when it is safe to do so. Non-punitive reporting systems protect people who report honest errors and hazards, while still holding individuals accountable for reckless behaviour — the balance of a just culture. Reports can be confidential or anonymous, and the programme should feed back what was learned and changed; reporting that disappears into a void stops quickly.

What to report: near-misses (a wire noticed late on approach, a door that opened in flight), equipment failures, medication errors, communication breakdowns, LZ problems, fatigue-related events, and any unsafe condition. Report promptly, factually and without blame: what happened, where, when, contributing factors, and suggestions.

The NASA Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) accepts confidential reports from anyone in aviation; filing a report within 10 days of an incident can provide limited protection from FAA penalties for unintentional violations. Many programmes also participate in industry databases and safety networks to share lessons.

Aircraft accidents (death or serious injury, or substantial damage to the aircraft) and certain serious incidents must be reported immediately to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in the United States, which investigates to determine probable cause and makes safety recommendations. The FAA enforces regulations and may also investigate. Preserve wreckage and records, and do not disturb the scene except to rescue people.

Medical events also have reporting pathways: medication errors, device malfunctions (the FDA MedWatch system), and patient harm (internal quality and risk management). Post-incident support — critical incident stress management and peer support — is part of a mature safety system.

On a night approach to a regular hospital helipad, the pilot sees a new construction crane late and makes an abrupt turn to avoid it. Nobody is hurt. Back at base, everyone is shaken; someone suggests not mentioning it to avoid trouble.

A report is only valuable if it leads to learning. Safety teams triage reports by risk, investigate significant events with tools such as root cause analysis, and look for patterns across many reports — a single LZ with repeated near-misses, a recurring equipment fault, or fatigue clustering on certain shift patterns.

Actions follow the hierarchy of controls: eliminate the hazard, substitute something safer, engineer controls (a better latch), administrative controls (a procedure or checklist), and lastly personal protective equipment. Training alone is the weakest control because it relies on memory under pressure.

Close the loop: tell the reporter and the wider crew what was found and changed. Safety bulletins, monthly safety meetings and briefings at shift change keep everyone informed and show that reporting matters.

Air medical aircraft carry several radios: VHF aviation radios for air traffic control and airport traffic (118–137 MHz), VHF/UHF FM radios for ground agencies (EMS, fire, police and hospitals), satellite tracking and messaging, and the intercom linking pilot and crew headsets. A transponder squawks a code that identifies the aircraft on radar; 7700 is emergency, 7600 is lost communications and 7500 is unlawful interference. The aviation emergency frequency is 121.5 MHz.

Intercom discipline protects the pilot: keep transmissions brief, avoid talking when the pilot is on the radio or during critical phases (sterile cockpit), and know how to isolate the crew intercom from the pilot during patient care. Agree on terms in advance — for example, "hold" (stop talking), "say again", and how the pilot announces critical phases.
Medical crew often handle communications with ground units, receiving hospitals and medical control, freeing the pilot to fly and talk to ATC.

Standard phraseology reduces misunderstanding in noisy, crowded radio environments. Think before you key the microphone, press and pause before speaking, speak clearly at a moderate rate, and release. Use "who you are calling, who you are, where you are, what you want": "Mercy Base, Life Flight 2, ten miles west, landing in five." Use plain language for medical content; avoid codes that receiving agencies may not share.

The ICAO phonetic alphabet: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu. Numbers are spoken digit by digit, with "niner" for 9 and "tree" for 3 in some regions. Common words: "Roger" (received), "Wilco" (will comply), "Affirmative", "Negative", "Say again", "Standby", "Over" and "Out".

Emergency calls: "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday" for distress (grave and imminent danger, immediate assistance required), "Pan-Pan, Pan-Pan, Pan-Pan" for urgency (a condition concerning safety that does not require immediate assistance). In a medical context, a deteriorating patient needing priority handling may be communicated to ATC as "medevac" or "lifeguard" in the call sign.

Flight following tracks the aircraft's position throughout the mission — by satellite tracking (automatic position reports every few minutes) and verbal position reports to the communications centre (typically every 15 minutes). If a scheduled report is missed and the aircraft cannot be contacted, the centre begins the overdue aircraft or post-accident incident plan.

A radio patient report should be short and structured: who you are and your ETA, age and sex, chief complaint or mechanism, key findings and vital signs, interventions and response, and specific requests (team activation, blood, cath lab, CT). For example: "City General, Life Flight 2, ETA 12 minutes with a 54-year-old male, inferior STEMI, BP 96/60, heart rate 52, on oxygen, aspirin and heparin given; request cath lab activation." Avoid patient names on open channels.

If communications fail: try other radios and frequencies, relay through another aircraft or ground unit, use phones or satellite messaging, and follow lost-communication procedures. The pilot squawks 7600 if ATC communication is lost.

You are working in the communications centre. A helicopter on a night scene flight missed its 15-minute position report. The satellite tracker shows its last position 6 minutes ago, stationary over a rural area away from the planned LZ. Calls on the company frequency are unanswered.

Ground agencies use their own radio systems, talk groups and terminology. Agree frequencies or talk groups during the request, and make sure the LZ coordinator can hear and speak to the aircraft. Use plain language rather than local codes, and keep instructions short.

Early notification of the receiving hospital allows teams to be ready: trauma team activation, cath lab, stroke team, blood, or a specific bed. Update the ETA as it changes. On landing at a hospital, confirm who receives the handover and give a structured report (for example MIST for trauma: Mechanism, Injuries, Signs, Treatment; or SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation).

Online medical control may be needed for orders outside protocol. Have the key information ready before calling, state the question clearly, and repeat back any orders to confirm. Document the time, the physician's name and the orders given.

Most deaths and serious injuries in survivable helicopter accidents result from head injury and occupants striking the cabin interior. Restraints work only if they are worn: crew should be seated and restrained with shoulder harnesses during take-off, landing and taxi, and whenever possible in flight. Unrestrained crew in the back of a helicopter have been associated with markedly higher injury and death rates.

Helmets reduce the risk of fatal head injury in crashes, protect hearing and support communication; visors protect eyes from bird strike and debris. Flame-resistant flight suits (such as Nomex), sturdy boots and gloves add protection from post-crash fire. Hearing protection matters because helicopter cabins often exceed 90–100 dB.

Crashworthy seats absorb vertical impact energy (stroking seats), and crash-resistant fuel systems reduce post-crash fire. Medical crew should know how to release their harness quickly — including when inverted — and the location of emergency exits.

The patient must be restrained on the stretcher with shoulder and lap straps, and the stretcher locked into a certified mount. Check the lock visually and physically before every flight. An unrestrained patient or stretcher becomes a projectile in turbulence or a hard landing, injuring the patient and crew.

All medical equipment — monitors, ventilators, pumps, oxygen cylinders, bags — must be secured to approved mounts or stowed. Loose items can strike crew, block exits, or interfere with flight controls. Equipment brought by a referring facility (balloon pumps, ECMO, incubators) must have an approved mounting solution before flight; if it cannot be secured, it cannot fly.

Oxygen cylinders are secured upright or in brackets, valves protected. Sharp items go into secured sharps containers. Infusion lines and tubes should be managed so that they do not snag during loading or egress.

A combative patient in flight can strike the pilot, controls or doors and endanger the aircraft. Assess the risk before departure: intoxication, psychosis, head injury, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia and pain all cause agitation. Treat the cause where possible, and use adequate chemical sedation (and intubation if needed) before flight rather than relying on physical restraints in the air.

Physical restraints should be soft, applied to all four limbs if used, and never prone — prone restraint can cause positional asphyxia and cardiac arrest. Monitor restrained patients continuously: airway, breathing, circulation, and distal perfusion of restrained limbs. Document the indication, type, time and checks.

Law enforcement custody patients may need an officer to accompany them if policy allows, and handcuffs must be removable by the crew in an emergency (keys on board) or replaced with soft restraints. Weapons are never allowed on board except per specific policy for law enforcement.
A 28-year-old with a scalp laceration and a GCS of 13 after a fall is intoxicated, shouting and pulling at his collar. He is protecting his airway. The flight to the trauma centre is 30 minutes.

Children and infants need age-appropriate restraint: approved child restraint devices or paediatric restraint systems for the stretcher, never held in a parent's arms during flight. Neonates travel in a secured transport incubator with internal restraints.

Pregnant patients are restrained with the lap belt below the abdomen across the pelvis and the shoulder strap between the breasts, with left lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression. Bariatric patients need stretchers and restraints rated for their weight and dimensions; standard straps may not fit safely.

Patients with spinal precautions are secured on a vacuum mattress or scoop that is itself locked to the stretcher. Patients with mental health crises who are calm should still be assessed for flight risk — sudden agitation in the aircraft is dangerous, and sedation or ground transport may be safer.

The pilot is responsible for the airworthiness inspection, but medical crew take part in a daily walk-around, often with the pilot, and check the cabin before every flight. Look for: fluid leaks, damage to the skin, rotor blades and tail rotor, open or unlatched panels and doors, foreign objects near the aircraft or in intakes, condition of tyres or skids, and tie-downs and covers removed. Report anything unusual — the pilot decides its significance.

In the cabin: seats and harnesses serviceable, helmets present and working (communications, visor), emergency exits clear and their release handles understood, fire extinguisher present and charged, first aid and survival kit present, lighting working, and the stretcher mount and locks functional.
After the walk-around, remove covers, tie-downs and any equipment from around the aircraft. A final "foreign object" check before start-up prevents rotor wash from lifting debris into the rotors.

Check all medical equipment at the start of each shift: monitor/defibrillator (charge, pads, cables, self-test), ventilator (function test, circuits, oxygen supply), suction (power and function), infusion pumps, video laryngoscope and airway kit, ultrasound, medications (stock, expiry, controlled drug count and security), blood products (temperature logs) and point-of-care testing equipment. Batteries should be fully charged with spares; aircraft power inverters checked.

Oxygen supply: check main and portable cylinder pressures and calculate duration. For US cylinders: duration (minutes) = (cylinder pressure in psi − safe residual, usually 200 psi) × cylinder factor ÷ flow (L/min). Common factors: D cylinder 0.16, E 0.28, M 1.56, H/K 3.14. A ventilator's oxygen use depends on minute ventilation and FiO₂ plus any driving gas; plan at least twice the expected flight time.
Configure the aircraft for the expected mission (neonatal incubator, balloon pump, bariatric stretcher) and confirm that all extra equipment is secured and accounted for in weight and balance.

Before each mission, the crew briefs: the mission (destination, patient, special equipment), weather and any concerns, fuel and possible refuelling, LZ or destination hazards, crew roles for the flight, and the plan for an in-flight emergency. Each crew member confirms readiness — including fitness for duty.

Checklists prevent omissions when people are tired, busy or interrupted; they do not replace knowledge but protect against memory failures. Use them for start-up, pre-departure ("doors closed and latched, belts on, equipment secured, ready for take-off"), and before landing. Read-do or challenge-and-response formats both work if used consistently.

A pre-departure "last look" by each crew member around their side of the aircraft — doors, latches, tie-downs and people clear — is a final barrier against common incidents such as doors opening in flight.

During the morning check, you notice a small fresh puddle of red fluid under the helicopter's transmission area, a cabin door latch that does not fully close, and a portable E cylinder showing 600 psi.

At shift change, the outgoing crew hands over aircraft and equipment status: any defects reported, items used and restocked, oxygen levels, controlled drug counts, blood products and their expiry, and any outstanding maintenance. The incoming crew completes their own checks rather than relying on the handover alone.

Readiness also means personal equipment: helmet fitted and tested, flight suit and boots, hearing protection, NVGs tested if used, personal survival kit, and phone or radio charged. A short team briefing at the start of the shift covers weather for the day, aircraft status, any known hazards (new construction, closed hospitals) and crew wellbeing.

Response time targets push crews to launch quickly, but a well-organised check at the start of the shift makes rapid, safe launches possible. Shortcuts at the start of the shift become problems at 03:00.

US regulations require that passengers are briefed before flight. For air medical operations, everyone who is not crew — family members, observers, students, accompanying providers and, when possible, the patient — receives a briefing covering: approaching and leaving the aircraft (only when directed, from the front or side, never near the tail), seat belts and harnesses (how to fasten and release), no smoking, use of helmets or headsets and how to talk on the intercom, location and operation of emergency exits, the fire extinguisher, survival equipment and first aid kit, the ELT, flotation devices for flights over water, and the brace position.

Passengers must not touch controls, door handles or medical equipment, must stay seated and belted, and must not distract the pilot — especially during take-off and landing. Explain what will happen in an emergency and that they must follow crew instructions immediately.
Briefings may be supplemented by printed cards, but a verbal briefing with a check of understanding is the standard. Document that the briefing was given.

Allowing a parent to accompany a child, or a family member to accompany a patient, can reduce distress and help consent and history-taking. But each additional person adds weight, takes space and may become a second patient or a distraction. Programmes have criteria: the person must be calm, sober, able to follow instructions, within weight limits, not need medical care themselves, and fit in an approved seat without impeding patient care or exits.

The final decision rests with the pilot (weight, balance and safety) and the medical crew (impact on patient care). A distraught or intoxicated family member should travel by ground. In a deteriorating situation — for example a cardiac arrest in flight — the crew should tell the family member what is happening and what they need from them.

Students, observers and accompanying providers (a neonatal nurse, a perfusionist) must be trained or briefed in aircraft safety and their role. Specialist teams such as ECMO crews need extra briefing on aircraft limits for their equipment.

Conscious patients should be briefed in simple terms: what the flight will be like (noise, vibration, cold), how long it will take, that they are strapped in for safety, how to signal pain or nausea, and what to do in an emergency. This reduces anxiety, which itself raises oxygen demand and heart rate.

Children respond to calm, honest, age-appropriate explanation; a parent's presence helps when it can be done safely. People who are deaf or hard of hearing need visual communication — writing boards, gestures agreed before take-off — because headsets may not help. Interpreters may be needed for patients and family who do not speak the crew's language; arrange this before departure, as cabin noise makes interpretation in flight difficult.
Patients with cognitive impairment or dementia may become distressed in the unfamiliar, noisy environment; carers can advise on what helps. Plan sedation or restraint needs before departure.

A 3-year-old with severe croup needs transfer. Her mother is calm, weighs 70 kg, and wants to fly. The pilot confirms there is weight margin and a certified seat. The father, who has been drinking, also asks to come.

Under the 2014 FAA rule, operators must brief medical personnel on aircraft safety before flight, or ensure they have completed training that covers it. Topics include: the aircraft's physical characteristics, approach and departure procedures, emergency exits and equipment, the location and use of fire extinguishers, oxygen system shut-off, and communication procedures with the pilot.

Accompanying specialists from a referring hospital — a perfusionist, a neonatal team, a paediatric intensivist — may be unfamiliar with aircraft. Brief them with the same rigour as passengers, plus their role during flight and any equipment limits (power, mounting, weight).
At the end of the briefing, ask for questions and confirm understanding of the most important items: how to release the belt, where the exits are, and when to stay silent.

Since the 2014 FAA rule, US helicopter air ambulance pilots must complete a pre-flight risk analysis before each flight. Risk assessment tools score factors such as weather (ceilings, visibility, forecast trends, icing), time of day and lighting, terrain, familiarity with the area and LZ, crew experience and fatigue, aircraft equipment (NVGs, IFR capability, autopilot), mission type (scene versus interfacility), and duty time.

Scores fall into bands: low risk (go), medium risk (mitigate and possibly seek approval from an operations control specialist or manager) and high risk (decline unless mitigated to an acceptable level, with management approval). Mitigations include waiting for weather to improve, using a different route or aircraft, adding an IFR plan, using a ground team, or changing the destination.

The analysis is completed without knowledge of the patient's condition and repeated when conditions change. A completed risk form is not a box to tick: it is a structured conversation about whether the flight should happen.

Crew resource management (CRM) is the effective use of all available resources — people, equipment and information — to achieve safe operations. It grew from aviation accident investigations showing that most accidents involved failures of communication, leadership, decision-making and situational awareness rather than technical skill.

Core skills: situational awareness (knowing what is happening, what it means and what will happen next), communication (closed-loop: send, acknowledge, confirm), leadership and followership, workload management, and decision-making. Assertive communication gives every crew member a voice; frameworks such as the "two-challenge rule" (if a concern is raised twice and not addressed, the crew member may take action to ensure safety) and graded assertiveness (CUS: "I'm Concerned, I'm Uncomfortable, this is a Safety issue") help junior crew speak up.

Threat and error management (TEM) anticipates threats (weather, terrain, fatigue, unfamiliar LZs, complex patients), traps errors before they cause harm, and manages undesired aircraft or patient states. Debriefing after missions — what went well, what could be better — builds a learning culture.

Risk changes during a mission: weather deteriorates, a scene LZ turns out to be tighter than described, fuel is lower than expected, or fatigue sets in. Reassess at each phase and set "decision points" in advance — for example, a minimum ceiling at which the aircraft will turn back.

Decision traps include plan continuation bias ("get-there-itis") — the tendency to continue a plan despite changing conditions, which strengthens as the destination nears; sunk cost thinking; mission pressure from a critically ill patient; and normalisation of deviance, in which small rule-bending becomes routine because nothing bad has happened yet.
A culture where any crew member can call "abort" without explanation or criticism — and where management supports conservative decisions — is the most effective defence.

Returning from a scene at night with a critically injured child, the ceiling ahead lowers and light rain begins. The trauma centre is 15 minutes away; a community hospital is 5 minutes away. The pilot says, "We're nearly there — I think we can make it."

A risk matrix combines likelihood (rare to almost certain) and severity (negligible to catastrophic) to rank hazards and decide responses. Applied to a flight, the pilot and operations control specialist use the programme's risk tool to identify the highest-scoring factors, then ask whether each can be reduced — by delaying, choosing another route, adding a second pilot, or using a ground team.

Operations control centres (OCCs), required for larger US HAA operators, provide a second person with weather and flight-tracking tools who participates in launch decisions, monitors flights and initiates the post-accident plan if needed. The OCC specialist can and should question a launch that looks risky.
Decision-making improves when information is shared openly: weather turn-downs by other services, LZ concerns from ground crews and recent near-misses should all feed into risk decisions.

Night vision goggles are image intensifiers: they collect ambient light (starlight, moonlight, cultural lighting) including near-infrared, convert photons to electrons at a photocathode, multiply the electrons through a microchannel plate, and strike a phosphor screen that produces a green (or white phosphor) image. They need some light — in total darkness or under heavy cloud with no ground lights, performance falls sharply.

NVGs improve the ability to see terrain, obstacles, weather and other aircraft at night and have been associated with reduced night accident risk in helicopter air ambulance operations. The 2014 FAA rule allows lower weather minimums when NVGs or HTAWS are used in some circumstances.

Limitations: a field of view of about 40° (compared with nearly 180° for the naked eye), visual acuity of about 20/25 to 20/40 at best, reduced depth perception, no colour discrimination, and degraded images in rain, fog, snow and smoke. Moving the head is essential to compensate for the narrow field.

White light inside the cabin "blooms" the goggles, washing out the image and forcing the tubes to shut down (automatic brightness control), and destroys the pilot's night adaptation. NVG-compatible lighting uses filtered blue-green light that the goggles do not detect. Medical crew must use only NVG-compatible lights in flight and cover or dim monitor screens, pump displays and other light sources; switch off unnecessary screens and use filters.

If white light is essential (for example, a procedure in flight), warn the pilot first ("white light in the cabin") and wait for acknowledgement; the pilot may need to change phase of flight or use the instruments. Agree these procedures in the pre-flight brief.

Medical crew members who wear NVGs act as additional lookouts during low-level flight and landing, calling out obstacles, wires and terrain using standard phraseology. They need initial and recurrent NVG training, including goggle adjustment (focus, eye relief, interpupillary distance) and pre-flight testing.

Halos form around bright light sources and can obscure objects nearby. Wires remain very hard to see; poles and towers give clues. Reduced depth perception and absent colour make it difficult to judge distance and closure rate — scan the instruments and use radar altimeters. Brownout and whiteout are harder to manage with NVGs because of the narrow field.

Fatigue increases with goggle use: neck strain from the weight on the helmet, eye strain and the mental effort of interpreting a monochrome image. The "dark adaptation" of the unaided eye (needed when looking under the goggles at instruments or outside) takes 20–30 minutes and is lost with any bright white light.

Scanning technique: move the head deliberately to sweep the field (the eyes alone cannot move far within a 40° view), look under or around the goggles to the instruments, and use off-centre viewing with the unaided eye in low light, because the centre of the retina (cones) is less sensitive at night than the periphery (rods).
During an NVG flight at 500 feet, the ventilator alarms for high pressure. You need to see the screen clearly and check the patient's chest and tube, which needs light.

Before flight, goggles are tested in a test lane or with a resolution chart: focus each tube, set the interpupillary distance, adjust eye relief and tilt, check for scintillation (sparkle), black spots, shading and distortion, and confirm battery levels with a spare battery. A goggle that fails any check is not used.

Goggles are mounted on the helmet with a counterweight to reduce neck strain. They should be stowed or flipped up during ground operations near bright lights and when white light is needed. Store and handle them carefully — the tubes are expensive and easily damaged.

Initial and recurrent training cover NVG theory, limitations, illusions, emergency procedures (goggle failure, transitioning to unaided flight), and crew coordination. Crew who use NVGs only occasionally are less proficient; currency requirements exist for pilots and are good practice for medical crew.

The Global Positioning System uses a constellation of satellites (about 31 operational) in medium Earth orbit. Each transmits its position and a precise time signal. A receiver calculates its distance from each satellite from the signal travel time; signals from at least four satellites give a three-dimensional position (latitude, longitude, altitude) and correct the receiver's clock. Other constellations (GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou) improve coverage when receivers use them.

Accuracy is typically within a few metres; augmentation systems such as WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) improve accuracy and integrity enough to fly instrument approaches. Errors arise from satellite geometry (poor dilution of precision when satellites are bunched), signal reflection off buildings and terrain (multipath), atmospheric delays, obstruction in valleys and urban canyons, and interference or jamming.

RAIM (receiver autonomous integrity monitoring) checks the consistency of signals and alerts the pilot when the position cannot be trusted. Databases must be current — an outdated database can show obstacles, frequencies and procedures that no longer match reality.

Latitude measures north–south position from the equator (0–90° N or S); longitude measures east–west position from the prime meridian (0–180° E or W). Coordinates can be written as degrees–minutes–seconds (35° 12' 30" N), degrees and decimal minutes (35° 12.50' N — the format most aviation GPS units use) or decimal degrees (35.2083° N — the format most phones use). Mixing formats is a common source of error — always state the format.

One degree of latitude is about 60 nautical miles; one minute is about 1 nautical mile; one second is about 30 metres. An error in the minutes or seconds column can put a helicopter in the wrong valley. Confirm coordinates by reading them back, and cross-check with a landmark, road name or mile marker.

Other location systems include the US National Grid / MGRS used by some public safety agencies, what3words, and street addresses. Scene coordinates from mobile phones are often accurate, but phone-reported locations at the time of a 911 call may be approximate. When the location is uncertain, ask ground crews for a landmark and to describe what the aircraft will see.

Moving-map displays show the aircraft's position over terrain, obstacles, airspace and LZ databases; synthetic vision systems render a 3D view of terrain ahead, useful in poor visibility. Tablets running aviation apps are widely used for situational awareness. All rely on accurate databases and power; a failure should not leave the crew lost.

Backup navigation includes VFR sectional charts, pilotage (navigating by visible landmarks such as roads, rivers and railways), dead reckoning (calculating position from heading, speed and time), and radio navigation aids (VOR). Medical crew can help with landmark identification and reading maps, especially when approaching unfamiliar scenes.

Over-reliance on automation ("automation complacency") reduces situational awareness. Cross-check the GPS against what you see and expect: if the screen says the LZ is on the left but the fire engines are on the right, trust your eyes and query the coordinates.

Dispatch gives scene coordinates as "36 15 30 north, 82 40 15 west". The pilot enters 36° 15.30' N, 82° 40.15' W. On arrival, there is no sign of the incident; ground crews report they can hear the helicopter somewhere to the south-east.

VFR sectional charts show terrain (contour lines and colour shading), obstacles (towers with their height above mean sea level and above ground level), airspace boundaries, airports and heliports, navigation aids and major landmarks. The maximum elevation figure in each grid shows the highest terrain or obstacle in that area, plus a margin.

Helicopter route charts and local LZ databases add hospitals, helipads and pre-surveyed landing sites. Obstacles shown on charts are only those that have been reported; new or temporary structures (cranes, wind turbines under construction) may not appear.

Medical crew should be able to locate the aircraft on a chart, identify obstacles near an LZ, and help the pilot cross-check landmarks. In an emergency or if the pilot is busy, giving a position relative to a charted landmark ("five miles north of the lake, over the highway") can be invaluable.

The Paediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) is a 30-second, hands-off look from the doorway at three components: appearance (tone, interactiveness, consolability, look or gaze, speech or cry — "TICLS"), work of breathing (abnormal sounds, retractions, nasal flaring, head bobbing, positioning such as tripoding or sniffing), and circulation to the skin (pallor, mottling, cyanosis). Appearance reflects brain perfusion and oxygenation and is the most important single element.

The pattern of abnormal components suggests the physiological problem: abnormal work of breathing alone suggests respiratory distress; abnormal work of breathing plus abnormal appearance suggests respiratory failure; abnormal circulation alone suggests compensated shock; abnormal circulation plus appearance suggests decompensated shock; abnormal appearance alone suggests a primary brain problem, metabolic or toxic cause. All three abnormal suggests cardiopulmonary failure.
After the PAT, perform the primary assessment (ABCDE with hands-on vital signs), then secondary assessment and history (SAMPLE), including birth history and immunisations for young children.

Children compensate for shock by increasing heart rate and systemic vascular resistance; blood pressure is maintained until about 25–30 % of circulating volume is lost, and hypotension is a late, pre-arrest sign. Early signs: tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill (more than 2 seconds), cool extremities, weak peripheral pulses compared with central pulses, decreased urine output and altered mental status. The hypotension threshold for ages 1–10 years is a systolic below 70 + (2 × age in years).

Respiratory failure in children often follows a period of distress with increasing work of breathing; fatigue leads to a falling respiratory rate, decreasing effort, altered consciousness and bradycardia — ominous signs that precede arrest. In infants, bradycardia is usually a response to hypoxia. Treat hypoxia first.

Weight estimation: use a length-based tape (such as the Broselow) or parent-reported weight; formulas (for example (age + 4) × 2 kg for ages 1–10) are less accurate. Accurate weight is the foundation of drug and fluid dosing.

Children's chest films look different: the thymus can widen the upper mediastinum in infants (the "sail sign"), the heart appears relatively large, and films are often taken supine and rotated. Look for hyperinflation and peribronchial thickening (bronchiolitis, asthma), focal consolidation (pneumonia), pneumothorax, foreign body (asymmetric inflation — the obstructed side may be hyperinflated on expiratory films), and ETT position (the tip should sit midway between the thoracic inlet and the carina, about T2–T3).

Ultrasound avoids radiation and is useful for FAST in trauma (though less sensitive in children because solid organ injuries often occur without free fluid), lung ultrasound, cardiac function and effusion, and vascular access. Neck soft tissue films show the "steeple sign" in croup and the "thumb sign" in epiglottitis, but a child with suspected epiglottitis should not be sent for X-ray — secure the airway in a controlled setting.

Capillary blood gases are commonly used in children and reflect pH and PCO₂ reasonably well if perfusion is good; they do not reflect oxygenation. Glucose must be checked in every sick child: infants have small glycogen stores and become hypoglycaemic quickly when ill.

A 4-month-old with 2 days of vomiting and diarrhoea is "sleepy". From the doorway: limp, not tracking faces, mottled skin, breathing fast but without retractions. HR 196, capillary refill 4 seconds, BP 74/40, glucose 2.4 mmol/L.

Parents notice subtle changes before monitors do: "She's not herself", "He stopped feeding", "She's too quiet". Take these concerns seriously — parental concern is an independent predictor of serious illness in children. Ask what the child is usually like and what has changed.

Assess young children on a parent's lap where possible, start with the least invasive observations (breathing, colour, behaviour from a distance), and save distressing procedures for last. A calm child gives a more accurate respiratory rate, heart rate and work of breathing; a screaming child's findings are hard to interpret.

Explain to the family what you are doing and why, in plain language. Ask about the child's past medical history, birth history in infants, immunisations, medications, allergies and recent illness. These details shape both diagnosis and destination.

Haemoglobin is high at birth (about 14–20 g/dL) because of fetal haemoglobin, falls to a physiological nadir of about 9–11 g/dL at 2–3 months as fetal cells are replaced, then rises gradually to adult values by adolescence. A haemoglobin of 10 g/dL may be normal at 2 months but abnormal at 2 years.

White cell counts are higher in infants and young children, with a lymphocyte predominance from about 1 month to 4–6 years. Neutropenia (an absolute neutrophil count below 1.0 × 10⁹/L, severe below 0.5) in a febrile child — often during chemotherapy — is an emergency requiring antibiotics within an hour. Platelet counts are similar to adults.
Coagulation tests are mildly prolonged in neonates because of immature liver synthesis; vitamin K is given at birth to prevent haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

Hypoglycaemia: in children, a glucose below about 3.0–3.3 mmol/L (54–60 mg/dL) is treated; in neonates, thresholds vary by age in hours, but levels below about 2.6 mmol/L (47 mg/dL) are commonly treated. Treat with 10 % dextrose 2–5 mL/kg IV or IO (0.2–0.5 g/kg). Avoid concentrated dextrose (25–50 %) in small children and neonates because of vein damage and rebound. In neonates, 10 % dextrose 2 mL/kg followed by an infusion is typical. Look for causes: sepsis, inborn errors of metabolism, adrenal insufficiency, toxins (alcohol, beta-blockers, sulfonylureas), and hyperinsulinism.

Sodium: hyponatraemia in children can be caused by hypotonic fluids, gastroenteritis, SIADH (meningitis, pneumonia, bronchiolitis) and water intoxication (dilute formula). Seizures from acute hyponatraemia need 3 % saline 2–5 mL/kg (up to 100–150 mL). Hypernatraemic dehydration (often from inadequate feeding in breastfed infants or excessive losses) must be corrected slowly — no faster than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour (10–12 mmol/L per day) — to avoid cerebral oedema.

Potassium: haemolysed capillary samples often give falsely high potassium; repeat on a free-flowing sample before treating if the ECG is normal. Hyperkalaemia occurs with renal failure, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (with hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia in a newborn) and tumour lysis syndrome.

Blood gas norms are similar to adults beyond the neonatal period. Children with chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia) may have chronically raised PCO₂ with metabolic compensation; know their baseline. A normal or rising PCO₂ in a child with asthma who is breathing fast is a warning sign of fatigue.

Inflammatory markers (CRP, procalcitonin) help risk-stratify febrile infants: elevated procalcitonin raises the likelihood of serious bacterial infection. Febrile infants under 28 days need full sepsis evaluation and antibiotics regardless of appearance. Lactate above 2 mmol/L supports sepsis or hypoperfusion.

Neonatal jaundice: unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin rises in the first days of life; levels above age-in-hours thresholds need phototherapy, and very high levels risk kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy). Jaundice in the first 24 hours is always pathological (haemolysis), and conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (pale stools, dark urine) suggests biliary atresia or liver disease.
A 10-day-old boy is lethargic and vomiting, with poor feeding. Glucose 2.0 mmol/L, sodium 124, potassium 7.1, HR 190, capillary refill 4 seconds. The genitalia appear normal.

Blood volume in children is small — about 80–90 mL/kg in infants — so repeated sampling can cause iatrogenic anaemia in neonates. Prioritise the tests that change management, and use point-of-care devices that need small volumes. Capillary samples (heel in infants, finger in children) give glucose, gas and some electrolytes, but squeezing causes haemolysis.

IO access provides samples for blood gas, glucose, electrolytes, haemoglobin and cross-match, although values (particularly potassium and some cell counts) may differ slightly from venous values. Label the sample source.
Interpret results against the child's age and the time of sampling relative to treatments: a glucose after a dextrose bolus or a potassium after salbutamol nebulisers will not reflect the baseline.

Almost every paediatric drug is weight-based, and errors are common: ten-fold errors (a misplaced decimal point), using pounds instead of kilograms, confusion between mg and mL, and wrong concentrations. Use a length-based tape or cognitive aid with pre-calculated doses, state the dose and volume aloud, have a second person check high-risk drugs (closed-loop: "Epinephrine 0.15 mg — that's 1.5 mL of 0.1 mg/mL"), and never exceed adult maximum doses.
Draw up only what you need in an appropriately sized syringe, label every syringe, and flush small volumes carefully — dead space in IV lines can hold a significant fraction of a small child's dose.

Pharmacokinetics differ: neonates and infants have more total body water (larger volume of distribution for water-soluble drugs), less fat, lower protein binding, immature hepatic enzymes (slower clearance of many drugs) and immature renal function. Toddlers often metabolise drugs faster than adults. Use age-appropriate references.
