Cardiac arrest: epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL), maximum 1 mg, every 3–5 minutes. Amiodarone 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg) or lidocaine 1 mg/kg for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT. Defibrillation 2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg, up to 10 J/kg or the adult dose. Synchronised cardioversion 0.5–1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg. Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg (max 6 mg), then 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg), for SVT. Atropine 0.02 mg/kg (no minimum dose in current guidance; max 0.5 mg) for vagal bradycardia.

RSI: ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV or etomidate 0.3 mg/kg; rocuronium 1 mg/kg (higher in shock) or succinylcholine 2 mg/kg in infants (1–1.5 mg/kg in older children). Infants are prone to bradycardia during laryngoscopy, mostly from hypoxia; have atropine ready. Avoid succinylcholine in undiagnosed myopathies (risk of hyperkalaemic arrest).

Vasoactive drugs: epinephrine (0.05–1 mcg/kg/min) or norepinephrine for fluid-refractory septic shock — cold shock often responds to epinephrine, warm shock to norepinephrine. Dopamine is no longer first line. Peripheral or IO infusions are acceptable initially in children.

Children are often under-treated for pain. Intranasal fentanyl (1.5 mcg/kg via an atomiser, max 100 mcg) works within minutes without IV access. Ketamine (0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV for analgesia; 1–1.5 mg/kg IV or 4 mg/kg IM for procedural sedation) preserves airway reflexes and breathing. Paracetamol (15 mg/kg) and ibuprofen (10 mg/kg) are effective for mild to moderate pain. Use age-appropriate pain scales (FLACC for preverbal children, faces scales for young children).

Seizures: benzodiazepine first line — midazolam 0.2 mg/kg IM or intranasal (max 10 mg), 0.3 mg/kg buccal, or 0.1 mg/kg IV; lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV. Second line: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg), fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, or valproate 40 mg/kg. Respiratory depression is more likely after repeated benzodiazepine doses.

Common transport infusions such as sedation after intubation use morphine or fentanyl with midazolam, or dexmedetomidine; propofol infusions are avoided for long-term sedation in children because of propofol infusion syndrome.
A 3-year-old (length-based tape: 14 kg) in pulseless VT after a drowning. The team prepares epinephrine 1 mg/10 mL (0.1 mg/mL), amiodarone and defibrillation.

Many drugs can be given without an IV. Intranasal (via an atomiser, up to about 1 mL per nostril): fentanyl, midazolam, ketamine, naloxone and dexmedetomidine. Intramuscular: epinephrine for anaphylaxis (anterolateral thigh), midazolam for seizures, ketamine for sedation, naloxone, ceftriaxone. Buccal midazolam for seizures. Rectal diazepam or paracetamol where other routes are unavailable.

Intraosseous access delivers any IV drug or fluid with similar onset and dose; the proximal tibia is the usual site in children, with the distal femur and humerus as alternatives. Flush with saline after each drug; IO infusion may need a pressure bag or syringe push.
Endotracheal drug administration is no longer recommended when IV or IO access is possible, because absorption is unpredictable.

Blood pressure cuffs should cover about 80–100 % of the arm circumference with a bladder width of about 40 % of the circumference; a cuff too small over-reads and too large under-reads. Non-invasive BP is particularly unreliable in small, moving, vasoconstricted children; trends, capillary refill and mental status add essential information.

Pulse oximetry probes designed for the child's size (wraps for infants, placed on a foot or palm) reduce motion artefact. Look at the waveform: a poor plethysmograph means the number may be wrong. Pre-ductal (right hand) and post-ductal (foot) saturations differ in some congenital heart disease and pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.

Waveform capnography is the standard for confirming and monitoring tracheal tube position in children of all sizes; use paediatric or neonatal adaptors with low dead space. Small tidal volumes and high respiratory rates can make sidestream readings lower than true values. ECG electrodes sized for children, placed away from the area where defibrillation pads may be needed.

Set alarm limits by age rather than leaving adult defaults: a heart rate of 60 is normal for an adolescent but an emergency in an infant; a respiratory rate of 40 is normal for a newborn but abnormal in a teenager. Programmes often use age-banded alarm presets.

In flight, vibration and noise make it impossible to hear alarms and difficult to examine the child. Position monitors where they can be seen, use visual alarms, and reassess the child directly — chest movement, skin colour and mental status — at regular intervals.

Trends matter more than single values. A slowly rising heart rate, increasing respiratory rate or widening gap between core and peripheral temperature over a flight are early signs of deterioration that a single reading may miss.

Infants and small children lose heat quickly: a large surface area relative to body mass, little subcutaneous fat, a large head, and (in neonates) reliance on non-shivering thermogenesis from brown fat, which consumes oxygen and glucose. Cold stress increases oxygen consumption, causes hypoglycaemia and acidosis and worsens outcomes.

Prevent heat loss: keep the child covered (including the head), warm the cabin, use warming mattresses or chemical warmers (with a barrier), warm IV fluids and minimise exposure during assessment. Monitor temperature continuously in critically ill infants (skin or rectal probe) and at least at departure and arrival in all children.
Avoid overheating as well: hyperthermia increases metabolic demand and may worsen brain injury. Febrile children should not be bundled excessively; antipyretics treat discomfort.

A 2-year-old with pneumonia is on high-flow nasal cannula. Thirty minutes into the flight, the monitor shows SpO₂ 94 %, HR 165 (up from 140), RR 52 (up from 40). The pleth trace is poor. Nobody heard an alarm because the limits were left at adult defaults.

Nasal-oral capnography cannulas measure end-tidal CO₂ in spontaneously breathing children. They detect hypoventilation during sedation well before desaturation, show the respiratory rate accurately, and give an early warning of obstruction (a shark-fin waveform in bronchospasm, loss of waveform in apnoea or obstruction).

In DKA, a low EtCO₂ reflects the degree of respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis; a rising EtCO₂ in an exhausted child with asthma or bronchiolitis suggests fatigue. In cardiac arrest, EtCO₂ reflects the quality of chest compressions and a sudden rise suggests return of spontaneous circulation.
Low-flow sidestream sampling suits small children; mainstream sensors add dead space and weight to small tubes. Combine capnography with direct observation — no monitor replaces looking at the child.

Stridor indicates upper airway narrowing. Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), usually viral (parainfluenza), affects children from about 6 months to 3 years with a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, often worse at night. Severity is graded by stridor at rest, retractions, air entry, cyanosis and consciousness (the Westley score). Treat all severities with dexamethasone 0.15–0.6 mg/kg orally or IV (max 10–16 mg); moderate to severe croup with nebulised epinephrine (0.5 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL, max 5 mL), which works within minutes but wears off in 2 hours — observe for rebound. Keep the child calm, with a parent, in a position of comfort.

Epiglottitis — now rare because of Hib vaccination but still seen in unvaccinated children and adults — presents with sudden high fever, toxic appearance, drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod positioning and soft stridor. Do not lie the child down, examine the throat or cause distress. The airway is secured in a controlled setting by the most experienced operator, with surgical airway backup. Bacterial tracheitis follows a viral illness with high fever, toxic appearance and thick secretions; many need intubation.

Foreign body aspiration peaks in toddlers: sudden choking, then cough, stridor or wheeze, sometimes unilateral reduced breath sounds. Complete obstruction requires back blows and chest thrusts (infants) or abdominal thrusts (children), then direct laryngoscopy and Magill forceps if unsuccessful.

Bronchiolitis, most often caused by RSV, affects infants under 2 years: coryza, then cough, tachypnoea, retractions, crackles and wheeze, peaking around days 3–5. Treatment is supportive — nasal suction, oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 90–92 %, hydration (nasogastric or IV), and high-flow nasal cannula (about 1–2 L/kg/min) or CPAP for increasing work of breathing. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics do not help routinely. Apnoea is a risk in young infants (under 2 months) and premature babies. Watch for fatigue, apnoea and rising CO₂.

Acute severe asthma: cannot complete sentences, accessory muscle use, SpO₂ below 92 %, peak flow below 50 % predicted; life-threatening features include silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion and normal or rising PCO₂. Treat with oxygen, repeated or continuous salbutamol (albuterol), ipratropium in the first hour, systemic steroids (prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg or dexamethasone 0.3–0.6 mg/kg), IV magnesium 40–50 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes, and IV salbutamol or epinephrine for refractory cases.

Intubation in asthma is high-risk: use ketamine, a large tube, low respiratory rate, short inspiratory time and long expiratory time, accept permissive hypercapnia, and disconnect and compress the chest if the patient becomes hypotensive from air trapping.

Distressed children are often best kept calm with a parent rather than separated for procedures. Decide before departure whether the child's trajectory allows transport on current support: rising oxygen needs, worsening work of breathing, apnoeas, a rising PCO₂ or exhaustion suggest escalation (NIV or intubation) before flight.

High-flow and CPAP devices must be compatible with the aircraft; calculate oxygen consumption (high-flow uses a lot). Altitude lowers the inspired oxygen partial pressure, so expect oxygen needs to rise in unpressurised aircraft.
Croup treated with nebulised epinephrine may rebound within 2 hours; ensure dexamethasone has been given and have more epinephrine available.

A 6-week-old, born at 34 weeks, with RSV bronchiolitis on high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min and FiO₂ 0.5. SpO₂ 91 %, RR 70 with marked retractions. In the past hour, two apnoeas with bradycardia needed stimulation. Capillary PCO₂ 68.

Anaphylaxis can cause upper airway swelling (stridor, hoarseness), bronchospasm (wheeze), hypotension and gastrointestinal symptoms after an allergen — food is the commonest trigger in children. Give IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (maximum 0.5 mg) into the anterolateral thigh immediately and repeat every 5 minutes as needed. Add fluids for hypotension and nebulised salbutamol for wheeze; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, not first-line treatment.

Refractory anaphylaxis needs an epinephrine infusion. Airway swelling may make intubation difficult — prepare for a surgical or needle airway. Biphasic reactions can occur hours later, so children are observed after treatment.

Hereditary angio-oedema causes swelling without urticaria and does not respond to epinephrine; it needs C1 esterase inhibitor or bradykinin-pathway drugs. Families usually know the diagnosis and carry treatment.

Non-accidental trauma is a leading cause of injury death in infants. Clinicians recognise it through mismatches: a history that does not explain the injury, a history that changes or differs between caregivers, a mechanism inconsistent with the child's developmental stage (for example, a non-mobile infant who "rolled off"), or an unexplained delay in seeking care.

Injury patterns that raise concern include any bruise in a non-mobile infant ("those who don't cruise rarely bruise"), bruises on the torso, ears, neck, buttocks or genitals (the "TEN-4" rule — torso, ears and neck in a child under 4, or any bruise in an infant under 4 months — is a validated screening tool), patterned bruises or burns resembling an object, immersion burns with clear lines and sparing of flexed areas, multiple injuries at different stages of healing, and certain fractures (posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal "corner" fractures, and fractures in non-ambulatory infants).

None of these is proof. Medical conditions (bleeding disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta, congenital dermal melanocytosis that resembles bruising) can mimic abuse. The transport clinician's role is to recognise concern, treat, document and report — not to investigate or confront.

Abusive head trauma (previously "shaken baby syndrome") typically affects infants under 1 year and causes subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages and brain injury, sometimes with rib or metaphyseal fractures and few external signs. Presentations range from vomiting, irritability and poor feeding (often mistaken for a viral illness) to seizures, apnoea, a bulging fontanelle and coma.

Management follows the principles of paediatric TBI: airway and ventilation (normocapnia), avoid hypoxia and hypotension, treat seizures, head up 30° and midline, hypertonic saline for signs of raised ICP, and transport to a paediatric trauma centre with neurosurgery. Check glucose. A full skeletal survey, ophthalmology examination and other investigations occur at the receiving centre.
Any infant with an unexplained apnoea, seizure or altered consciousness should have abusive head trauma considered, particularly if the history is vague.

Document objectively and precisely: what you saw (size, colour, location and shape of injuries), what you were told, by whom, and in their own words in quotation marks. Avoid judgements ("abused child") and speculation. Body diagrams help. Record times and who was present.

Healthcare providers are mandated reporters: reasonable suspicion of abuse must be reported to child protective services or law enforcement according to local law — proof is not required, and good-faith reports are legally protected. Inform the receiving team so that the hospital's child protection team is involved. Siblings and other children in the home may also be at risk.

Remain professional and non-confrontational with caregivers. Accusations can escalate conflict and compromise the child's safety or the investigation. Explain what you are doing for the child; decisions about whether a caregiver accompanies the child follow normal safety criteria and any instructions from law enforcement.

A 3-month-old is referred with "vomiting and a seizure, probably viral". The parent says the baby rolled off a sofa yesterday. On examination: bulging fontanelle, GCS 9, a small bruise behind the left ear and another on the chest. CT shows bilateral subdural collections of different densities.

Non-accidental injury is not limited to bruises and head trauma. Abdominal injuries (duodenal haematoma, pancreatic and liver injury) can present with vomiting and abdominal pain without external bruising. Burns, poisoning with medicines or drugs, neglect (malnutrition, untreated illness) and fabricated or induced illness (where a caregiver causes or invents symptoms) are other forms.

Older children may disclose abuse to a clinician. Listen calmly, do not ask leading questions, reassure them that they were right to tell, and do not promise to keep it secret — explain that you must tell people who can help. Record their words exactly.
Caring for abused children is distressing. Debrief with your team, use peer support or employee assistance programmes, and recognise that strong emotions are normal responses to these cases.

Dehydration is graded by clinical signs: mild (3–5 %) with few signs; moderate (6–9 %) with dry mucous membranes, reduced tears, sunken eyes or fontanelle, reduced urine output, tachycardia and slightly prolonged capillary refill; severe (10 % or more) with lethargy, cool mottled skin, capillary refill over 3 seconds, deep (acidotic) breathing, weak pulses and eventually hypotension. Prolonged capillary refill, abnormal skin turgor and abnormal respiratory pattern are the most useful individual signs.

The best measure is weight loss from a recent known weight: each 1 % of body weight lost equals about 10 mL/kg of fluid deficit. Most children with mild to moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis can be rehydrated orally or by nasogastric tube; IV fluids are for severe dehydration, shock, persistent vomiting or altered consciousness.
Check glucose and electrolytes in children needing IV fluids, particularly infants and those with altered mental status.

Shock: give 10–20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid (balanced solution or 0.9 % saline) over 5–20 minutes and reassess after each bolus — heart rate, capillary refill, mental status, blood pressure, liver edge and lung sounds. Stop and consider inotropes if signs of fluid overload appear (hepatomegaly, crackles, rising work of breathing). Use smaller boluses (5–10 mL/kg) in cardiac disease, DKA and severe malnutrition. Up to 40–60 mL/kg may be needed in the first hour of septic shock where intensive care is available; in resource-limited settings without ICU, large boluses have caused harm (FEAST trial). Haemorrhagic shock needs blood (10–20 mL/kg) after an initial crystalloid bolus or sooner.

Maintenance fluids (Holliday–Segar, the 4-2-1 rule): 4 mL/kg/hour for the first 10 kg, plus 2 mL/kg/hour for the next 10 kg, plus 1 mL/kg/hour for each kg above 20 kg. A 25 kg child needs 40 + 20 + 5 = 65 mL/hour. Many acutely ill children (those with pneumonia, bronchiolitis, meningitis, post-operative) have raised ADH and should receive about two-thirds of this to avoid fluid overload and hyponatraemia.

Use isotonic maintenance fluids (for example 0.9 % saline or a balanced solution with 5 % dextrose): hypotonic fluids (such as 0.18 % saline) have caused fatal hyponatraemic encephalopathy in children, and the AAP recommends isotonic fluids with appropriate potassium chloride and dextrose for most children aged 28 days to 18 years.

Hyponatraemic dehydration (sodium below 135) results from replacing losses with water or hypotonic fluids. Symptoms appear with rapid falls or levels below about 125: headache, vomiting, lethargy, seizures. Seizures need 3 % saline 2–5 mL/kg. Otherwise correct with isotonic fluid and monitor sodium every 2–4 hours, aiming for a rise of no more than 8–10 mmol/L per day.

Hypernatraemic dehydration (sodium above 145–150) occurs with excessive water loss or inadequate intake (breastfeeding problems in neonates, diarrhoea with concentrated feeds). The child may look less dehydrated than they are, with doughy skin and irritability. Correct slowly over 48 hours (no more than about 0.5 mmol/L per hour) to avoid cerebral oedema and seizures.

Hypokalaemia from vomiting and diarrhoea causes weakness and arrhythmias; potassium is added to maintenance fluids once urine output is confirmed. Hypocalcaemia in infants (from vitamin D deficiency or hypoparathyroidism) presents with seizures, tetany or stridor (laryngospasm).
An 18-month-old (11 kg) with 3 days of diarrhoea and vomiting: lethargic, mottled, capillary refill 4 s, HR 180, RR 40 deep, BP 80/50, sunken fontanelle. Glucose 3.4, sodium 131, bicarbonate 12.

Peripheral access is difficult in shocked, dehydrated or small children. Limit peripheral attempts in critical situations: if access fails within about 90 seconds or two attempts in a child in shock or arrest, place an intraosseous needle. Ultrasound-guided peripheral access improves success in difficult cases.

IO sites: proximal tibia (1–2 cm below the tibial tuberosity on the flat medial surface), distal femur, and proximal humerus in older children. Complications include extravasation (compartment syndrome), dislodgement and, rarely, osteomyelitis. Secure the needle carefully for transport and check the limb regularly.
Measure fluid volumes precisely in small children: use burettes or syringe pumps rather than free-flowing bags, which can deliver large volumes unnoticed during a flight.

DKA is defined by hyperglycaemia (glucose above 11 mmol/L, 200 mg/dL), venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15 (18 in some guidelines), and ketonaemia or ketonuria. Severity: mild (pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15), moderate (pH < 7.2 or bicarbonate < 10), severe (pH < 7.1 or bicarbonate < 5). About a third of children present with DKA at diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, often after symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) were missed.

Signs: dehydration (often overestimated clinically), vomiting, abdominal pain (mimicking appendicitis), deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing, a ketotic smell and altered consciousness. Young children, those with new diabetes and severe DKA are at the greatest risk of complications.

Measure glucose, blood gas, electrolytes (calculate corrected sodium), urea and creatinine, ketones and, where possible, calcium, phosphate and magnesium. Weigh the child. An ECG or monitor helps detect potassium abnormalities.

Fluids: if in shock, give 10–20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid; otherwise a 10 mL/kg bolus over 30–60 minutes is common. Then replace the deficit (typically estimated at 5–10 %) plus maintenance evenly over 24–48 hours with isotonic fluid. The PECARN FLUID trial (2018) found that neither the rate of rehydration nor the sodium content of fluids within the studied range changed the rate of clinically apparent brain injury — shifting focus from fluid restriction to careful, evenly paced rehydration.

Insulin: start an infusion of 0.05–0.1 units/kg/hour 1–2 hours after fluids have begun; no bolus. Aim for glucose to fall by about 3–5 mmol/L per hour; add dextrose (5–10 %) when glucose falls below about 14–17 mmol/L (250–300 mg/dL) and continue insulin until acidosis resolves. Do not stop insulin to correct falling glucose — add more dextrose instead.

Potassium: total body potassium is depleted even when serum levels are normal or high; insulin drives potassium into cells. Add potassium (typically 40 mmol/L) once the serum level is known and urine output is present, unless above 5.5. Hypokalaemia below 3.5 should be corrected before insulin. Bicarbonate is not given except for life-threatening hyperkalaemia; it increases the risk of cerebral oedema.

Cerebral oedema occurs in about 0.5–1 % of paediatric DKA, usually 4–12 hours after treatment starts, and carries high mortality and morbidity. Risk factors: young age, new-onset diabetes, severe acidosis, low PCO₂, high urea, a failure of measured sodium to rise as glucose falls, and bicarbonate treatment. Warning signs: headache, vomiting, irritability or reduced consciousness, inappropriate slowing of heart rate, rising blood pressure, incontinence and abnormal posturing.

Treat immediately, without waiting for a CT: mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg over 10–15 minutes or 3 % saline 2.5–5 mL/kg, reduce the fluid rate, elevate the head, and support the airway (avoiding hyperventilation except for signs of herniation). Intubation is high-risk in severe acidosis because patients rely on hyperventilation to compensate — match their minute ventilation after intubation.

Inborn errors of metabolism usually present in neonates or infants after feeding begins or during illness: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures, unusual odour, hypoglycaemia, metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap, or hyperammonaemia (with respiratory alkalosis). Stop protein feeds, give 10 % dextrose at 1.5 times maintenance to stop catabolism, treat hypoglycaemia, and transfer to a centre with metabolic specialists. Many families carry an emergency letter for known conditions.

A 7-year-old (22 kg) with new diabetes: glucose 32 mmol/L, pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4, PCO₂ 14, sodium 132, potassium 5.1. Three hours after fluids and insulin began, he complains of headache, becomes irritable, and his heart rate falls from 128 to 76 while BP rises.

Before departure, document the start time of fluids and insulin, the volumes given, and the latest glucose, gas and electrolytes. Use separate infusion pumps for insulin, maintenance fluids with potassium, and dextrose so that each can be adjusted independently (the "two-bag system" uses two bags with different dextrose concentrations to adjust glucose without changing the total rate).

Check capillary glucose hourly in flight and neurological status at least hourly. A falling glucose below target means adding dextrose, not stopping insulin. Hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia are the commonest complications of treatment.

Children with DKA and a reduced level of consciousness need a gastric tube for vomiting and aspiration risk. Intubation is avoided where possible because of the risks described; if needed, the most experienced operator performs it with careful ventilation targets.

Children with special healthcare needs have chronic physical, developmental, behavioural or emotional conditions requiring more care than usual. They are over-represented among transports. The most valuable resource is the caregiver, who knows the child's baseline — usual vital signs, oxygen requirement, neurological status, communication and what "unwell" looks like for them. Ask: "What is different from normal today?"

Emergency information forms (and portable care plans) summarise diagnoses, medications, allergies, devices, baseline examination and specific emergency instructions. Ask for them early. Children with complex conditions may have unusual drug requirements, contraindications (for example, succinylcholine in muscular dystrophies) or known difficult airways.

Children with autism spectrum disorder may be very sensitive to noise, light and touch, and an aircraft is a sensory assault. Explain simply, use the child's preferred communication method, allow comfort objects, minimise unnecessary touch and noise (ear defenders help), and let a caregiver stay close. Agitation may be distress rather than defiance. Children with developmental delay may not localise or report pain; use behavioural pain tools and the caregiver's interpretation.

Cerebral palsy: spasticity, scoliosis and contractures make positioning, IV access and airway management harder; many have seizures, gastrostomy tubes, aspiration risk and chronic lung disease. Baclofen pump failure or abrupt withdrawal causes rebound spasticity, fever and potentially life-threatening autonomic instability.

Children with neuromuscular disorders (muscular dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy) have weak respiratory muscles and cough, may use home non-invasive ventilation, and deteriorate quickly with respiratory infections. Avoid succinylcholine (risk of hyperkalaemic arrest) and volatile agents. Ventilator-dependent children are covered in the high-tech lesson.

Down syndrome: congenital heart disease, airway obstruction (large tongue, small midface, subglottic stenosis — use a smaller ETT), atlanto-axial instability (avoid neck extension), hypothyroidism and an increased risk of leukaemia.

Sickle cell disease: vaso-occlusive pain crises (early opioid analgesia, fluids, oxygen if hypoxic), acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate with fever, chest pain or hypoxia — oxygen, antibiotics, incentive spirometry, transfusion), splenic sequestration (rapidly enlarging spleen with falling haemoglobin and shock in young children — careful transfusion), stroke (urgent exchange transfusion), aplastic crisis (parvovirus) and sepsis (functional asplenia — fever over 38.5 °C needs urgent antibiotics). Altitude and dehydration can precipitate sickling; maintain oxygenation and hydration in flight.

Oncology patients: febrile neutropenia (antibiotics within 1 hour), tumour lysis syndrome (hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, renal failure — fluids, avoid potassium, treat hyperkalaemia), superior mediastinal mass (anterior mediastinal tumours can cause complete airway or cardiovascular collapse with sedation or supine positioning — keep the child upright and avoid sedation and paralysis where possible), hyperleucocytosis, and spinal cord compression. Central lines (ports, tunnelled catheters) are the preferred access but carry infection risk; use strict asepsis.

Haemophilia: treat bleeds early with the child's factor concentrate (families often carry it and know the dose); head injuries, neck swelling and iliopsoas bleeds are emergencies. Avoid IM injections and NSAIDs.

A 9-year-old with autism and a femur fracture is screaming and hitting out when touched. His mother says he is non-verbal, hates loud noise and bright light, and calms with his tablet and weighted blanket. The flight is 40 minutes.

Children with medical complexity often have multiple specialists, devices and medications, and frequent hospital admissions. Advance care plans may specify limits on interventions or preferred hospitals; check for them and respect them, while confirming the current wishes of the family.

Many of these children have unusual "normal" values — chronic hypoxaemia in cyanotic heart disease, compensated respiratory acidosis in neuromuscular disease, low muscle tone, or baseline tachycardia. Treat the child relative to their own baseline, not textbook norms.

Transport may be needed to the child's usual specialist centre rather than the nearest hospital, because their records, team and equipment are there. Discuss destination with the family and receiving teams before departure when the child's condition allows.

Children's tracheostomy tubes are small (often 3.0–5.0 mm internal diameter), frequently uncuffed, and easily blocked by secretions. The commonest emergencies are obstruction and accidental decannulation. Caregivers are usually skilled and carry an emergency kit with a spare tube of the same size and one size smaller, suction catheters, ties and a syringe.

For a child in distress with a tracheostomy: give oxygen to the face and the stoma, suction the tube (to the pre-measured depth, often written on the kit), and if suction will not pass or the child does not improve, change the tube immediately — a blocked tube is the most likely cause. If the same size will not go in, insert the smaller tube. If no tube can be placed, cover the stoma and ventilate by bag-mask over the mouth and nose (if the upper airway is patent), or apply a small mask or neonatal mask to the stoma.

Children with a tracheostomy because of upper airway obstruction (for example, subglottic stenosis) may be impossible to intubate or ventilate from above — know why the tracheostomy was placed. A fresh tracheostomy (under about 1 week old) has an immature tract that can close or create a false passage; stay sutures may be present to help reopen it.

Home ventilators deliver pressure- or volume-controlled breaths via a tracheostomy or a mask (non-invasive). They are compact, have internal batteries and are often more reliable than people expect, but their circuits, humidifiers and power supply can fail. Caregivers know the usual settings and alarms.

When a ventilated child deteriorates, disconnect from the ventilator and hand-ventilate with a bag and oxygen, then work through DOPE: Displacement of the tube, Obstruction (secretions, kinked tube — suction and change if needed), Pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, rising pressures, hypotension), Equipment failure (ventilator, circuit, oxygen, power). If hand-ventilation improves the child, the problem was probably the equipment. Add "S" for stacked breaths (auto-PEEP) in asthma or obstructive disease.

For transport, the home ventilator can often be used if it is approved for the aircraft, its batteries are sufficient for twice the transport time, and the crew understands it — or the child is transferred to the transport ventilator with equivalent settings. Bring the caregiver's emergency bag, spare tubes, suction and the humidification device (heat and moisture exchanger).

Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunts drain CSF from the brain to the abdomen. Shunt malfunction (blockage, disconnection, infection) causes raised ICP: headache, vomiting, lethargy, irritability, a bulging fontanelle and increasing head size in infants, sunsetting eyes, and eventually bradycardia, hypertension and coma. Infection presents with fever, abdominal pain and redness along the shunt. Treat as raised ICP, image, and transfer to neurosurgery; the shunt may need emergency tapping by neurosurgery.

Gastrostomy tubes (G-tubes and button devices) can dislodge; the tract can begin to close within hours, so a replacement or a Foley catheter of similar size can be placed to keep it open if the tract is mature (usually older than 6–8 weeks). A new tract should not be re-instrumented — refer back to the surgical team.

Long-term central lines (tunnelled catheters, implanted ports) are used for chemotherapy, parenteral nutrition and long-term antibiotics. Fever in a child with a central line is presumed line infection until proven otherwise — take blood cultures and give antibiotics within 1 hour. Other emergencies: line occlusion, line fracture (clamp proximal to the break) and air embolism (clamp, left side down, oxygen).

A 3-year-old with a 4.0 uncuffed tracheostomy (for subglottic stenosis) on a home ventilator becomes agitated; SpO₂ falls to 78 %, HR 180, little chest movement. The ventilator alarms "high pressure".

Implanted cardiac devices (pacemakers and defibrillators) occur in children with congenital heart disease. Magnet placement disables defibrillator shocks and sets pacemakers to a fixed rate; do this only when indicated. Children with single-ventricle physiology (after Norwood, Glenn or Fontan operations) have specific oxygen saturation targets and are sensitive to changes in pulmonary vascular resistance — seek cardiology advice.

Insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors are common in children with diabetes; in DKA or severe illness the pump is usually stopped and IV insulin started. Vagal nerve stimulators for epilepsy can be activated with a magnet to abort seizures. Cochlear implants need the external processor protected.
Families are usually the experts on these devices. Bring device information cards, chargers and supplies with the child.

Sepsis in children is suggested by fever or hypothermia with tachycardia, tachypnoea, altered mental status, poor perfusion (prolonged capillary refill, mottling, cool peripheries or flash refill and bounding pulses in warm shock), and reduced urine output. Hypotension is late. Infants, children with chronic illness, immunosuppression or central lines are at highest risk. The 2024 Phoenix Sepsis Criteria define sepsis in children as suspected infection with life-threatening organ dysfunction across respiratory, cardiovascular, coagulation and neurological systems.

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign paediatric guidelines recommend: antibiotics within 1 hour for septic shock (and within 3 hours for sepsis without shock), blood cultures if they do not delay antibiotics, 10–20 mL/kg fluid boluses (up to 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour where intensive care is available) with reassessment after each, balanced crystalloids, and early vasoactive drugs — epinephrine or norepinephrine — for fluid-refractory shock, which can be started peripherally. Hydrocortisone is considered for catecholamine-refractory shock.

Check glucose and calcium and correct them. Lactate is useful for risk stratification. Intubation in septic shock can precipitate cardiovascular collapse; resuscitate first, use ketamine, and have adrenaline ready.

Bacterial meningitis in children presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting and altered consciousness; infants show non-specific signs — irritability, poor feeding, lethargy, a bulging fontanelle, hypothermia or seizures — and often no neck stiffness. Common organisms vary by age: group B streptococcus, E. coli and Listeria in neonates; Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis in older children.

Meningococcal septicaemia can progress within hours: a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash (the "glass test"), with shock, coagulopathy and multi-organ failure. Give antibiotics immediately — a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone (80–100 mg/kg) — without waiting for lumbar puncture or imaging; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage in neonates and vancomycin where resistant pneumococcus is common. Dexamethasone given with or before the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis and is used in many centres for bacterial meningitis beyond infancy.

Transport crews should use droplet precautions (surgical mask) for suspected meningococcal disease until 24 hours of effective antibiotics. Close contacts — including crew who performed unprotected airway procedures — may need chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin, rifampicin or ceftriaxone) per public health advice.

Falling vaccination rates have brought back diseases many clinicians have never seen. Measles is extremely contagious (airborne; it lingers in the air for up to 2 hours): prodrome of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, Koplik spots in the mouth, then a maculopapular rash spreading from the face downward. Complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and death, especially in infants and the malnourished. Use airborne precautions (N95 or equivalent) and ensure crew immunity.

Pertussis (whooping cough) is most dangerous in young infants, who may present with apnoea, cyanosis and bradycardia rather than the classic whoop; extreme leucocytosis and pulmonary hypertension predict death. Treat with macrolide antibiotics, support ventilation and use droplet precautions. Varicella can cause severe skin infection (group A streptococcus), pneumonia and encephalitis; it is airborne and contact transmitted. Diphtheria, polio and tetanus remain rare but are seen in under-vaccinated populations and travellers.

Other considerations: tuberculosis (airborne), multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) after COVID-19 (fever, shock, cardiac dysfunction, rash), and travel-related infections such as malaria in febrile children returning from endemic areas.
A 14-month-old with fever for 8 hours, now lethargic with cold peripheries, capillary refill 5 seconds, HR 190, BP 72/38, and spreading purple spots on the legs that do not fade under pressure.

Infants under 3 months with fever (38 °C or higher) have a significant risk of serious bacterial infection: urinary tract infection most commonly, then bacteraemia and meningitis. Their signs are subtle, and appearance is less reliable than in older children. Febrile infants under 28 days need full evaluation (blood, urine and CSF cultures) and empirical antibiotics; those aged 29–60 days are risk-stratified with inflammatory markers per guidelines.

Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection presents with fever or hypothermia, seizures, vesicles or sepsis-like illness in the first weeks of life and needs acyclovir. Hypothermia is as concerning as fever in neonates.
For transport, these infants need glucose monitoring, temperature control, cultures drawn before antibiotics if possible without delay, and early antibiotics.

Infants and young children have a large occiput (which flexes the neck when supine — place a towel under the shoulders), a large tongue, a higher and more anterior larynx (C2–C3 in infants versus C4–C6 in adults), a floppy, omega-shaped epiglottis, and a narrow airway in which small amounts of oedema cause large increases in resistance (resistance rises with the fourth power of the radius decrease). Infants are preferential nose breathers. They have a smaller functional residual capacity and higher oxygen consumption, so they desaturate quickly during apnoea.

A straight (Miller) blade lifting the epiglottis directly is often used in infants; a curved (Macintosh) blade in older children; video laryngoscopes with paediatric blades are increasingly standard. Cuffed tubes are now preferred for most children beyond the newborn period, with cuff pressure monitored and kept below 20–25 cmH₂O: they reduce tube changes and leaks without increasing complications. Size: cuffed (age ÷ 4) + 3.5 mm; uncuffed (age ÷ 4) + 4 mm; depth at the lip about 3 × the tube size.

Supraglottic airways (i-gel, LMA) come in weight-based sizes and are excellent rescue devices. Needle cricothyroidotomy is the surgical rescue for children under about 8–10 years, whose cricothyroid membrane is too small for a surgical cricothyrotomy.

Prepare everything sized in advance (length-based tape), position (shoulder roll in infants, ear-to-sternal notch alignment in older children), and preoxygenate with high-flow oxygen; apnoeic oxygenation via nasal cannula prolongs safe apnoea time. Resuscitate shock before induction with fluids and have epinephrine ready (push-dose or infusion).

Drugs: ketamine 1–2 mg/kg IV (haemodynamically stable choice), or etomidate 0.3 mg/kg; rocuronium 1–1.2 mg/kg or succinylcholine (2 mg/kg in infants). Atropine 0.02 mg/kg is not routine but is used for infants with bradycardia or when succinylcholine is repeated. Bradycardia during laryngoscopy in an infant usually means hypoxia — stop, oxygenate, then retry.

Limit attempts, call for help early, use a supraglottic airway as rescue, and confirm placement with waveform capnography. Secure the tube well — small movements in a short trachea cause displacement or endobronchial intubation. Note the depth at the lip and recheck after every move.

Lung-protective ventilation: tidal volume 5–8 mL/kg of ideal body weight (lower, 3–6 mL/kg, in paediatric ARDS with poor compliance), plateau pressure below 28–30 cmH₂O, PEEP 5 cmH₂O or higher as oxygenation requires, and the lowest FiO₂ that maintains SpO₂ around 92–97 % (88–92 % in severe ARDS). Respiratory rates by age: infants about 25–40, toddlers 20–30, school-age 15–25, adolescents 12–20. Adjust to EtCO₂ and blood gases; permissive hypercapnia is accepted in ARDS and asthma.

Pressure-control modes are commonly used in small children because they compensate for tube leaks; volume-control with a set tidal volume is also used, especially with cuffed tubes. Monitor delivered tidal volumes — circuit compliance and leaks affect small breaths more.

Troubleshooting follows DOPE(S): displacement (check depth, capnography), obstruction (secretions — small tubes block easily; suction), pneumothorax, equipment failure, and stacked breaths. In flight, re-check tube depth after loading, monitor cuff pressure on ascent (gas expansion), and keep a bag-valve device with a PEEP valve and appropriately sized mask at hand.

An intubated 18-month-old (cuffed 4.0 tube at 12 cm) with pneumonia desaturates to 80 % immediately after being loaded into the aircraft. Breath sounds are reduced on the left. EtCO₂ waveform present.

High-flow nasal cannula and CPAP or bilevel NIV can avoid intubation in many children with bronchiolitis, pneumonia and asthma. Signs of success within 1–2 hours include falling heart and respiratory rates and reduced work of breathing; failure signs include rising oxygen needs, worsening work of breathing, apnoeas, rising CO₂ and decreasing consciousness.

Interfaces must fit — nasal prongs, nasal masks, full-face masks and helmets come in paediatric sizes. Gastric distension from NIV can splint the diaphragm; a gastric tube helps. Agitated children may need light sedation (dexmedetomidine or low-dose ketamine) to tolerate NIV.

For transport, decide before departure whether NIV is likely to succeed for the duration of the flight. A child who is failing or borderline is safer intubated on the ground than in a confined, noisy cabin.

Gestational age guides almost every decision: viability (about 22–24 weeks), steroid and magnesium benefit, the receiving unit and the neonatal team needed. Use dates from an early ultrasound where available. Fundal height in centimetres approximates gestational weeks between about 20 and 36 weeks; at 20 weeks the fundus is at the umbilicus, and at 12 weeks it rises just above the pubic symphysis.

History: gravidity and parity (G3P2 = three pregnancies, two births beyond 20 weeks), prior caesarean (uterine rupture risk), complications in this pregnancy (pre-eclampsia, placenta praevia, diabetes, multiple pregnancy), rupture of membranes (time and colour of fluid — meconium staining), bleeding, contractions (frequency, duration, strength), fetal movements and prenatal care.

Physiological changes alter assessment: heart rate rises by 10–20 beats/min, blood pressure falls in the second trimester, blood volume increases by about 40–50 % (so significant blood loss may be hidden), there is a dilutional anaemia, a respiratory alkalosis (PaCO₂ about 30 mmHg), and from about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the vena cava when supine — tilt left or manually displace the uterus.

An external tocodynamometer, a pressure transducer strapped over the fundus, records the frequency and duration of contractions; it does not measure their strength (an intrauterine pressure catheter does). Contraction frequency is measured from the start of one contraction to the start of the next. Normal active labour has 3–5 contractions per 10 minutes.

Tachysystole is more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes, and can reduce placental blood flow and cause fetal distress — particularly with oxytocin. A hypertonic or tetanic contraction (lasting longer than 2 minutes, or with no relaxation between contractions) is an emergency that may signal abruption or uterine rupture; stop oxytocin and consider a tocolytic per protocol.

Imminent delivery: regular strong contractions every 2–3 minutes, an urge to push, rectal pressure, crowning or visible presenting part. Transport during active second-stage labour risks delivery in a cramped aircraft; it is often safer to deliver at the referring facility with neonatal support than mid-flight.

Normal fetal heart rate is 110–160 beats/min. Variability (fluctuations of 6–25 beats/min) indicates an intact fetal nervous system and adequate oxygenation; reduced or absent variability may reflect hypoxia, sleep, prematurity or maternal drugs (opioids, magnesium). Accelerations (rises of 15 beats/min for 15 seconds at term) are reassuring.

Decelerations: early decelerations mirror contractions (head compression) and are benign; variable decelerations are abrupt and vary in shape and timing (cord compression) and are concerning if deep, prolonged or recurrent; late decelerations begin after the contraction peak and return after it ends (uteroplacental insufficiency) and are concerning, especially with reduced variability. Prolonged bradycardia below 110 for more than 10 minutes is an emergency.

The three-tier NICHD system classifies tracings: Category I (normal — reassuring), Category II (indeterminate — needs evaluation and intrauterine resuscitation), and Category III (abnormal — absent variability with recurrent late or variable decelerations or bradycardia, or a sinusoidal pattern — needing urgent delivery). Intrauterine resuscitation: left lateral position, IV fluid bolus, oxygen if the mother is hypoxic, stop oxytocin, treat hypotension, and consider a tocolytic.

A 31-week G2P1 with preterm contractions is referred to a tertiary centre 45 minutes away by air. Contractions every 4 minutes, lasting 50 seconds; cervix 4 cm. FHR 145 with moderate variability and occasional early decelerations. She has received the first dose of betamethasone.

Trauma is a leading non-obstetric cause of maternal death. Resuscitating the mother is the best way to resuscitate the fetus: oxygen, left uterine displacement after 20 weeks, early blood, and avoiding hypotension. Maternal compensation can hide blood loss of 1–1.5 L, and the fetus may be the first to show maternal shock through an abnormal heart rate.

Even minor trauma can cause placental abruption, often hours later. Pregnant trauma patients beyond about 20–24 weeks are monitored with continuous cardiotocography for at least 4–6 hours at a facility able to manage obstetric complications. Rh-negative mothers receive anti-D, and a Kleihauer–Betke test quantifies fetal-maternal haemorrhage.

Pelvic binders, imaging and drugs are used as needed — necessary radiation should not be withheld. Seat belts should sit below the abdomen across the pelvis; abdominal bruising from a lap belt is a warning sign of uterine and placental injury.

Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, so haemoglobin falls (a level above about 10.5–11 g/dL is acceptable). White cells rise (up to about 15 × 10⁹/L, higher in labour). Platelets fall slightly (gestational thrombocytopenia, rarely below 70–80 × 10⁹/L). Pregnancy is hypercoagulable: fibrinogen rises to about 4–6 g/L at term, so a "normal" non-pregnant fibrinogen of 2 g/L is low in late pregnancy and predicts severe postpartum haemorrhage.

Renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rise by about 50 %, so creatinine falls (normal about 35–70 µmol/L, 0.4–0.8 mg/dL); a creatinine of 90 µmol/L (1.0 mg/dL), normal outside pregnancy, may indicate renal impairment. Blood gases show a compensated respiratory alkalosis (PaCO₂ about 28–32 mmHg, bicarbonate about 18–21 mmol/L), so a "normal" PaCO₂ of 40 in a pregnant woman with asthma suggests respiratory failure.
Alkaline phosphatase rises (placental origin); liver transaminases do not. Glucose tolerance worsens in later pregnancy; gestational diabetes is common.

Pre-eclampsia: proteinuria (protein:creatinine ratio ≥ 0.3 mg/mg, or ≥ 300 mg in 24 hours) or, in its absence, evidence of end-organ involvement — platelets below 100 × 10⁹/L, creatinine above 97 µmol/L (1.1 mg/dL) or doubling, transaminases twice normal, pulmonary oedema or neurological symptoms. HELLP syndrome: haemolysis (raised LDH above about 600 U/L, schistocytes, falling haemoglobin, raised bilirubin), elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT twice normal) and low platelets (below 100 × 10⁹/L).

Obstetric haemorrhage and DIC: falling haemoglobin lags behind blood loss; fibrinogen below 2 g/L is a key trigger for fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate or concentrate), and viscoelastic testing guides therapy where available. Placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, sepsis, retained dead fetus and severe pre-eclampsia can all cause DIC.

Magnesium therapy is monitored clinically (reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output) and with levels: therapeutic about 2–3.5 mmol/L (4–7 mEq/L); loss of reflexes about 5 mmol/L; respiratory depression about 6–7 mmol/L; cardiac arrest above about 12 mmol/L.

Rh-negative mothers exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood (trauma, bleeding, abruption, delivery) can form anti-D antibodies that harm future pregnancies. Anti-D immunoglobulin is given within 72 hours of a potential sensitising event. The Kleihauer–Betke test quantifies fetal cells in maternal blood to guide the anti-D dose; in trauma it also identifies feto-maternal haemorrhage.

Neonatal values: glucose (treated below about 2.6 mmol/L, 47 mg/dL, in many protocols); umbilical cord gases (an arterial pH below 7.0 or base deficit worse than −12 suggests significant intrapartum hypoxia and may qualify for therapeutic hypothermia); haemoglobin is high at birth (14–20 g/dL); and bilirubin rises over the first days (jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological).
Neonatal sepsis screening includes blood cultures, white cell count and CRP, with risk factors such as prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever and group B streptococcus colonisation.
A 34-week primigravida with epigastric and right upper quadrant pain, BP 158/104, headache. Labs: Hb 9.8, platelets 62, AST 310, ALT 280, LDH 890, creatinine 92 µmol/L, fibrinogen 2.6 g/L.

Maternal sepsis is a leading cause of maternal death. Normal pregnancy changes (raised heart rate, lower blood pressure, raised white cell count) blur the usual criteria, so obstetric-specific early warning scores are used. Lactate is not raised by normal pregnancy, although it rises in labour; a lactate above 2 mmol/L in a pregnant patient with suspected infection is concerning.

Common sources: chorioamnionitis, endometritis after delivery, pyelonephritis, wound infection and pneumonia. Group A streptococcus causes rapidly progressive, severe sepsis. Treat with early broad-spectrum antibiotics (within an hour), fluids and source control, and monitor the fetus.

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (third trimester; nausea, vomiting, jaundice, hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia) overlaps with HELLP but has more marked hypoglycaemia, liver failure and coagulopathy. It requires delivery and intensive care.

Magnesium sulfate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures and provides fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks. Loading dose 4–6 g IV over 15–20 minutes, then 1–2 g/hour. Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate (above 12), urine output (above about 25–30 mL/hour) and, where available, levels. Reduce the infusion in renal impairment. Toxicity: loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, cardiac arrest — stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10 %) IV over 3–10 minutes.

Severe hypertension (systolic ≥ 160 or diastolic ≥ 110 sustained for 15 minutes) is an emergency treated within 30–60 minutes to prevent stroke. First-line: IV labetalol (20 mg, then 40, then 80 mg every 10 minutes; avoid in asthma and heart failure), IV hydralazine (5–10 mg every 20 minutes), or oral immediate-release nifedipine (10–20 mg, repeated). Target about 140–150/90–100 — avoid precipitous drops that compromise placental flow.
ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated in pregnancy. Nitroprusside is a last resort because of fetal cyanide toxicity.

Tocolytics delay preterm labour for up to 48 hours to allow antenatal steroids and transfer: nifedipine (a common first choice; watch for hypotension), indomethacin (before 32 weeks; avoid longer than 48 hours because of ductal constriction and oligohydramnios), and terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously for short-term use (for example tachysystole) — it causes maternal tachycardia and is not used for prolonged tocolysis. Magnesium is not an effective tocolytic but is given for neuroprotection.

Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart, or dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for four doses) between about 24 and 34 weeks reduce neonatal death, respiratory distress syndrome and intraventricular haemorrhage. Benefit begins within hours, so the first dose should not be delayed for transfer.

Uterotonics for postpartum haemorrhage: oxytocin (10 units IM or IV infusion — avoid rapid IV bolus, which causes hypotension), methylergonovine (0.2 mg IM; contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia), carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α 250 mcg IM every 15–90 minutes; contraindicated in asthma), and misoprostol (600–1000 mcg orally, sublingually or rectally). Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth (repeat once after 30 minutes if bleeding continues) reduced death from bleeding in the WOMAN trial.

Ventilation is the most important intervention in neonatal resuscitation; drugs are rarely needed. Epinephrine for a heart rate below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation and 60 seconds of coordinated compressions: 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (0.2 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL; range 0.01–0.03 mg/kg), repeated every 3–5 minutes; endotracheal 0.1 mg/kg while access is obtained. Volume: 10 mL/kg of normal saline or O-negative blood for suspected hypovolaemia (pale, poor perfusion, history of blood loss).

Glucose: 10 % dextrose 2 mL/kg (0.2 g/kg) for hypoglycaemia, followed by an infusion of about 4–6 mg/kg/min (60–80 mL/kg/day of 10 % dextrose). Surfactant is given via the endotracheal tube for preterm respiratory distress syndrome. Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) 0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min keeps the ductus arteriosus open in duct-dependent congenital heart disease; it causes apnoea (prepare to ventilate), fever and hypotension.

Antibiotics for suspected neonatal sepsis: ampicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime/ceftazidime per protocol). Naloxone is not recommended in the delivery room for respiratory depression; support ventilation instead. Vitamin K 1 mg IM is given after birth.
A 36-week patient with severe pre-eclampsia is on magnesium 2 g/h. One hour into a ground-to-air transfer: reflexes absent, respiratory rate 9, SpO₂ 91 %, urine output 10 mL over the past hour.

Most emergency drugs can be used in pregnancy when needed — the mother's health comes first. Drugs to avoid or use cautiously: ACE inhibitors and ARBs (fetal renal toxicity), warfarin (teratogenic in the first trimester), NSAIDs after about 20 weeks (oligohydramnios, ductal constriction), tetracyclines, and valproate (neural tube defects). Opioids, paracetamol, most antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins), heparins, labetalol, nifedipine and standard resuscitation drugs are used routinely.

RSI in pregnancy: anticipate a difficult airway (oedema, large breasts, aspiration risk, rapid desaturation from reduced functional residual capacity and higher oxygen consumption). Preoxygenate well with head-up positioning, use a smaller tube, and use standard induction doses; succinylcholine and rocuronium are appropriate. Magnesium potentiates non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers.
Most drugs given to a breastfeeding mother are compatible with breastfeeding; for specific questions, consult the LactMed database.

Monitor the mother as any critical patient: ECG, blood pressure (cuff sized for the arm; in pre-eclampsia, frequent measurements or an arterial line), SpO₂, respiratory rate, temperature, urine output with a catheter, and capnography if sedated or intubated. Position in left lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression, which otherwise reduces cardiac output and placental perfusion.

Continuous electronic fetal monitoring in flight is limited by noise, vibration, space and the movement of the transducers; many programmes use intermittent auscultation with a handheld Doppler (fetal heart rate before departure, at intervals during transport and on arrival) and a tocodynamometer or manual palpation for contractions. Some transport monitors record both. Document the FHR baseline and any decelerations, and palpate contractions directly when in doubt.

Point-of-care ultrasound confirms fetal cardiac activity, presentation (cephalic or breech), placental location (praevia) and free fluid. It is useful before departure to anticipate breech delivery or confirm fetal demise.

A transport incubator (isolette) provides a thermally controlled, enclosed environment with a neonatal ventilator, oxygen and air supplies, suction, monitoring (ECG, SpO₂, temperature, non-invasive BP, often capnography), infusion pumps and battery power. It is mounted on a specialised stretcher and secured to the aircraft; together it is heavy and must be included in weight and balance.

Before each transport: pre-warm the incubator (to about 34–37 °C depending on the infant's size and gestation), check battery charge and aircraft power compatibility, gas supplies (and calculate duration), ventilator function, alarms, suction and the neonatal airway and resuscitation kit. Access ports allow care without opening the incubator, which loses heat quickly.

Servo-control mode adjusts heater output to the baby's skin temperature probe; air mode controls the air temperature. Secure the infant with internal straps or a nest, and keep lines and tubes visible and secured so they do not kink during loading.

Pre-ductal saturation (right hand) reflects blood reaching the brain; post-ductal (either foot) reflects blood past the ductus arteriosus. A difference of more than about 3 % (post lower than pre) suggests right-to-left shunting across the ductus — persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn or duct-dependent systemic circulation (for example coarctation or hypoplastic left heart).

Target pre-ductal SpO₂ in the first minutes of life rises gradually (about 60–65 % at 1 minute to 85–95 % by 10 minutes); afterwards most neonates are kept at about 90–95 %, with lower targets in some cyanotic congenital heart disease per cardiology advice. Avoid hyperoxia in preterm infants (retinopathy, lung injury).

Temperature: aim for an axillary temperature of 36.5–37.5 °C; check every 15–30 minutes in transport. Capnography (mainstream sensors are bulky; low-dead-space adaptors exist) confirms tube placement and helps titrate ventilation. Blood glucose is checked on departure and regularly in transport. Transcutaneous CO₂ monitoring is available in some services.
A term newborn with meconium aspiration is intubated. Right hand SpO₂ 92 %, foot 78 % on FiO₂ 1.0. BP 50/28 (mean 35). The infant becomes agitated with handling and saturations drop further.

At altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen falls. The fetus is relatively protected by fetal haemoglobin (which binds oxygen more tightly) and a left-shifted dissociation curve, but maternal hypoxia reduces fetal oxygen delivery. Give supplemental oxygen to keep maternal SpO₂ at or above about 95 % and consider requesting a lower cabin altitude in fixed-wing transport for compromised pregnancies.

Motion sickness and vomiting are common; antiemetics such as ondansetron or metoclopramide are used. Vibration and noise make auscultation impossible — rely on monitors with visual displays and Doppler devices. Restrain the pregnant patient with the lap belt below the abdomen and maintain left tilt with a wedge.

Plan for delivery in the aircraft even when it is unlikely: a delivery kit, neonatal resuscitation equipment, warming and a plan for who does what. In-flight delivery is rare but chaotic without preparation.

Cord prolapse — the cord descending through the cervix ahead of the presenting part after the membranes rupture — compresses the cord and cuts off fetal blood flow. Risk factors: malpresentation (breech, transverse), prematurity, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy and a high presenting part at rupture. Suspect it with sudden fetal bradycardia or variable decelerations after rupture, or when the cord is seen or felt.

Management aims to relieve pressure on the cord until caesarean delivery: call ahead, elevate the presenting part off the cord with a gloved hand in the vagina (and keep it there throughout transport), place the mother in knee–chest or steep Trendelenburg with left tilt, or fill the bladder with 500–750 mL of saline via a catheter to lift the presenting part. Minimise handling of the cord (to avoid vasospasm); cover an exposed cord with warm, moist dressings. Tocolysis (terbutaline) may reduce contractions.
If delivery is imminent and vaginal birth can be achieved quickly, deliver; otherwise, rapid transport to a unit able to perform immediate caesarean section.

Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally sited placenta: painful bleeding (although bleeding may be concealed), a tender, firm or "woody" uterus, frequent or tetanic contractions, fetal distress and maternal shock out of proportion to visible blood loss. Risk factors: hypertension and pre-eclampsia, trauma, cocaine, smoking and previous abruption. It causes DIC — check fibrinogen and give products early. Ultrasound often misses abruption; diagnosis is clinical.

Placenta praevia is a placenta covering or near the cervix: painless, bright red bleeding, a soft non-tender uterus, often in the third trimester. Never perform a digital vaginal examination when praevia is possible — it can provoke massive haemorrhage. Resuscitate with blood, give Rh immune globulin if Rh-negative, and transfer to a centre able to perform caesarean section.

Uterine rupture — most often in women with a previous caesarean scar during labour — presents with sudden abdominal pain, loss of fetal station, abnormal fetal heart rate (often bradycardia), cessation of contractions and maternal shock. It requires immediate laparotomy.

Shoulder dystocia: the head delivers but retracts against the perineum ("turtle sign") and the shoulders do not follow with gentle traction. Call for help, avoid fundal pressure and excessive traction, and use the McRoberts manoeuvre (hyperflex the mother's hips onto her abdomen) with suprapubic pressure; then internal rotational manoeuvres, delivery of the posterior arm, or moving the mother to all fours. HELPERR is a memory aid.

Breech delivery: allow the baby to deliver spontaneously to the umbilicus ("hands off the breech"), support the body, and deliver the head with flexion (the Mauriceau manoeuvre: fingers on the maxilla, flex the head, suprapubic pressure). Do not pull. A head that does not deliver within a few minutes is an emergency.

Postpartum haemorrhage (blood loss of 1000 mL or more, or any bleeding with signs of hypovolaemia) is a leading cause of maternal death. Causes — the four Ts: Tone (uterine atony, about 70 %), Trauma (lacerations, inversion, rupture), Tissue (retained placenta or products) and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Treat with fundal massage, uterotonics (oxytocin first), bimanual compression, TXA within 3 hours, blood products (with early fibrinogen) and rapid transfer for definitive control (balloon tamponade, embolisation, surgery).

A 33-week patient in transport has a sudden gush of fluid. The fetal heart rate falls from 145 to 80 and stays there. On inspection, a loop of cord is visible at the introitus. Landing is 20 minutes away.

Complicated deliveries often produce compromised newborns. After cord prolapse, abruption, shoulder dystocia or prolonged breech delivery, expect a baby who needs resuscitation: prepare warming, suction, a bag-mask with appropriately sized masks, pulse oximetry and a person dedicated to the newborn.

Shoulder dystocia can cause brachial plexus injury (Erb palsy) and clavicle or humerus fractures in the baby, and perineal trauma and PPH in the mother. Breech delivery risks head entrapment and hypoxia. Abruption can cause fetal anaemia and hypovolaemic shock in the newborn — 10 mL/kg of O-negative blood may be needed.

Document times precisely: time of the head delivering, time of the body, onset of resuscitation and Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes. These records matter for the receiving neonatal team and for therapeutic hypothermia decisions.

Dizygotic (fraternal) twins come from two eggs and always have two placentas and two amniotic sacs (dichorionic diamniotic). Monozygotic (identical) twins come from one egg that splits: depending on timing, they may be dichorionic diamniotic, monochorionic diamniotic (one shared placenta, two sacs — most common for identical twins) or monochorionic monoamniotic (one placenta, one sac — highest risk, including cord entanglement).

Monochorionic twins share placental circulation, which can be unbalanced: twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS) — one twin becomes the donor (anaemic, growth-restricted, oligohydramnios) and the other the recipient (polycythaemic, fluid-overloaded, polyhydramnios, heart failure). Multiple pregnancy increases risks of preterm labour (more than half of twins are born before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, anaemia, placenta praevia, malpresentation, cord prolapse and postpartum haemorrhage.
Triplets and higher-order multiples carry greater risks still; nearly all are born preterm and many need neonatal intensive care.

A woman in preterm labour with a multiple pregnancy is usually transferred before delivery to a centre with enough NICU capacity for all the babies — in utero transfer is safer than transferring several sick preterm neonates afterwards. Confirm that the receiving unit has cots for every baby. Give antenatal steroids, magnesium for neuroprotection (< 32 weeks) and tocolysis per protocol.

If delivery is imminent, it is safer to deliver at the referring hospital with neonatal teams present than in an aircraft. A transport team may be requested to retrieve multiple neonates afterwards; each critically ill neonate typically needs its own team and incubator, which may mean several teams or sequential transfers.
Prepare for each baby separately: resuscitation equipment, warming, staff and identification. Label babies and cords (Twin A, Twin B) and record the time of each birth.

The first twin is delivered as a singleton (the presenting twin is usually cephalic). After the first birth, clamp and cut the cord (labelled), and check the lie and heart rate of the second twin. Contractions often pause; the second twin may change position, and its cord may prolapse. The interval between births is ideally short (often within 30 minutes), as the risk of hypoxia for the second twin rises with time and placental separation.

If the second twin is cephalic or breech and descending, allow delivery with maternal effort; a transverse second twin needs obstetric manoeuvres (external or internal version) or caesarean section — another reason to deliver at a hospital where possible.

After delivery, the over-distended uterus contracts poorly: postpartum haemorrhage is more common. Give oxytocin after the last baby is delivered (not before — it could trap the second twin), massage the fundus, and be ready for the PPH bundle.

A 29-week monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy in preterm labour at a rural hospital: cervix 5 cm, contractions every 3 minutes, both fetal hearts reassuring. The nearest NICU with two available cots is 60 minutes by air.

Twins and triplets are often preterm and small, and each needs its own warming, resuscitation equipment and staff. Before delivery, set up separate resuscitation stations and assign teams. Monochorionic twins with TTTS may be born with opposite problems: the donor anaemic and hypovolaemic (may need blood), the recipient polycythaemic with heart failure (may need partial exchange and inotropes).
Identification is critical: label each baby and their samples clearly and consistently, record birth order and times, and ensure that the receiving unit receives correct information for each infant.

When transport resources are limited, prioritise the sickest infant for immediate transfer and arrange additional teams for the others; communicate clearly with parents about where each baby is going.

Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension (systolic ≥ 140 or diastolic ≥ 90 on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) after 20 weeks of gestation with proteinuria or, in its absence, evidence of end-organ dysfunction. It can also present for the first time postpartum, up to about 6 weeks after delivery. The cause is abnormal placentation leading to widespread endothelial dysfunction and vasospasm.

Severe features: systolic ≥ 160 or diastolic ≥ 110; platelets below 100 × 10⁹/L; liver transaminases twice normal or severe right upper quadrant/epigastric pain; creatinine above 97 µmol/L (1.1 mg/dL) or doubling; pulmonary oedema; and new headache unresponsive to medication or visual disturbances. Hyperreflexia and clonus suggest cerebral irritability.

Risk factors: first pregnancy, previous pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, renal disease, autoimmune disease, multiple pregnancy, obesity, age over 35 and IVF pregnancy. Definitive treatment is delivery of the placenta; until then, the aims are to prevent stroke, seizures and organ damage while planning timing and place of delivery.

Severe hypertension (≥ 160/110 sustained for 15 minutes) must be treated within 30–60 minutes: stroke is the leading cause of death in pre-eclampsia. IV labetalol (20, 40, then 80 mg every 10 minutes, up to 300 mg), IV hydralazine (5–10 mg every 20 minutes) or oral immediate-release nifedipine (10–20 mg) are first line. Aim for 140–150/90–100; overly rapid falls can compromise placental perfusion — monitor the fetal heart.

Magnesium sulfate prevents eclampsia in pre-eclampsia with severe features (and treats eclamptic seizures): 4–6 g IV over 15–20 minutes, then 1–2 g/hour, continued for 24 hours after delivery or the last seizure. Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output; reduce the dose in oliguria or renal impairment. Calcium gluconate 1 g IV reverses toxicity.

Fluids: pre-eclamptic women are at risk of pulmonary oedema from capillary leak, low oncotic pressure and diastolic dysfunction. Restrict total fluids (often about 80 mL/hour) and avoid large boluses unless haemorrhaging. Place a urinary catheter and record hourly output.

Eclampsia is a generalised seizure in a woman with pre-eclampsia (although up to a fifth of eclamptic seizures occur before hypertension or proteinuria are recognised, and some occur postpartum). Warning signs: severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain and hyperreflexia.

During a seizure: protect from injury, place in left lateral position, maintain the airway, give oxygen and suction. Most eclamptic seizures are brief and self-limiting. Give magnesium 4–6 g IV over 15–20 minutes (or 5 g IM into each buttock if no IV access); for recurrent seizures, give a further 2 g IV. Benzodiazepines are second-line if magnesium fails. Treat severe hypertension.

After the seizure, assess the fetus — bradycardia during and after a seizure usually recovers within minutes as maternal oxygenation improves; do not rush to delivery until the mother is stabilised. Consider other causes of seizures (intracranial haemorrhage, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, cerebral venous thrombosis, hypoglycaemia) if the seizure is atypical or recurrent. Persistent neurological deficit or reduced consciousness needs imaging.

During transfer of a 35-week patient with severe pre-eclampsia (BP 172/112, on magnesium 1 g/h after a 4 g load), she complains of worsening headache and then has a generalised seizure lasting 90 seconds. Fetal heart rate falls to 90.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) causes headache, visual disturbance, altered consciousness and seizures from vasogenic oedema in the posterior brain, associated with severe hypertension and endothelial dysfunction. It usually resolves with blood pressure control and delivery. Intracerebral haemorrhage — the most feared complication of severe hypertension in pregnancy — presents with sudden headache, focal signs or coma and needs urgent imaging and neurosurgical input.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is more common in pregnancy and the postpartum period (hypercoagulability, dehydration) and presents with headache, seizures and focal deficits. Stroke, hypoglycaemia, epilepsy and drug toxicity are other causes of seizures in pregnancy.

A seizure that is atypical (focal, prolonged, recurrent despite magnesium) or followed by persistent deficits needs imaging. Transport to a centre with neuroimaging, neurosurgery, obstetrics and intensive care.

Prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM) is rupture before the onset of labour at any gestation; at term it affects about 8 % of pregnancies, and most women labour within 24 hours. Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) is rupture before 37 weeks and before labour; it complicates about 3 % of pregnancies and causes about a third of preterm births. Prolonged rupture is more than 18–24 hours.

Diagnosis: history of a gush or continuous leak of fluid; sterile speculum examination showing pooling of fluid in the posterior vagina or leaking from the cervix with coughing; and tests such as nitrazine paper (alkaline amniotic fluid turns it blue — false positives with blood, semen and infection) or ferning on microscopy, or commercial protein tests. Avoid digital cervical examination in PPROM unless the woman is in active labour, because it increases infection risk and shortens latency.
Ultrasound may show reduced amniotic fluid (oligohydramnios). Note the colour of the fluid: meconium staining or blood-stained fluid alters management.

Infection: chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection) presents with maternal fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and foul-smelling fluid, and threatens both mother (sepsis) and baby (neonatal sepsis, cerebral palsy). It requires broad-spectrum antibiotics and usually delivery.

Cord prolapse is more likely, especially with malpresentation or a high presenting part. Placental abruption is also more common. Preterm birth follows in most cases of PPROM — about half deliver within a week — with the complications of prematurity. Very early PPROM (before about 24 weeks) risks pulmonary hypoplasia and limb deformities from prolonged oligohydramnios.
Signs of fetal compromise — variable decelerations from cord compression, bradycardia — need urgent assessment for cord prolapse and delivery.

At term, most women are offered induction of labour (or expectant management for a limited time); group B streptococcus prophylaxis is given if indicated. In PPROM without infection or fetal compromise, expectant management until about 34 weeks reduces prematurity complications: antibiotics to prolong latency (commonly ampicillin and erythromycin or azithromycin for 7 days — avoid amoxicillin-clavulanate, associated with necrotising enterocolitis), antenatal corticosteroids (24–34 weeks), magnesium for neuroprotection before 32 weeks if delivery is imminent, and GBS prophylaxis in labour. Tocolysis in PPROM is controversial and not routinely recommended.

Transport: women with PPROM are usually transferred to a centre with an appropriate NICU before delivery. Before departure, check for labour, cord prolapse, infection and fetal wellbeing. In flight, monitor maternal temperature, heart rate, contractions and fetal heart, and carry delivery and neonatal resuscitation equipment.
If chorioamnionitis is present, delivery is indicated regardless of gestation; antibiotics should be started before transfer, and the receiving neonatal team informed.

A 30-week patient with leaking fluid for 14 hours; speculum exam confirms pooling. Temperature 37.2 °C, HR 92, uterus non-tender, mild irregular tightenings. FHR 140 with moderate variability. The referring hospital has no NICU.

Group B streptococcus (GBS) colonises the genital tract of about a fifth to a quarter of pregnant women and is a leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (penicillin or ampicillin; cefazolin or clindamycin/vancomycin with penicillin allergy per protocol) is given to colonised women, those with unknown status and risk factors (preterm labour, prolonged rupture over 18 hours, intrapartum fever), and women with previous GBS-affected babies.

Neonates born after PROM or PPROM, maternal fever or chorioamnionitis are assessed for early-onset sepsis using risk calculators or clinical observation; symptomatic babies receive blood cultures and antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamicin).
Communicate maternal risk factors to the receiving neonatal team: duration of rupture, maternal temperature, GBS status and antibiotic timing.

Gestational (pregnancy-induced) hypertension is new hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ features; it can progress to pre-eclampsia, so it is monitored closely and severe-range pressures are treated in the same way. Chronic hypertension predates pregnancy or appears before 20 weeks; pre-eclampsia can be superimposed on it.

HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe variant of pre-eclampsia, sometimes without marked hypertension or proteinuria. Symptoms include right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting and malaise — often mistaken for gastritis or gallbladder disease. Complications: DIC, placental abruption, acute kidney injury, pulmonary oedema, and subcapsular liver haematoma or rupture (sudden severe pain, shock — a surgical emergency).
